[{SEASON}] The season of {FOOD} is upon your people. [Peak Season +2]
The wine cellars of Minas Tirith have not been restocked. Rations are thin and the men can feel it — the White City feels very far away tonight.
The Gondorian column is running dry. What little wine remains is set aside for the wounded. The men march on water and memory.
The last cask cracked three days ago. Gondorian soldiers do not complain — but they are quieter than usual, and that says everything.
The cellars of Minas Tirith have not run dry. Gondorian wine fills the mess cups tonight — duty tastes finer, and the men stand a little straighter.
A cask of Lebennin red cracked open among the soldiers. The grape harvest of the Pelennor feeds more than the body — it feeds the memory of what we are defending.
Faramir's quartermaster packed well. The wine of Gondor's vineyards runs in every cup, and for a moment the men forget the road is long.

The wagons are laden with Gondorian vintage — more than the march could reasonably need. The men are generous tonight, the cups never empty, and the White Tower seems close enough to touch. [Rations: Surplus]

Abundance from the vineyards of Lebennin. Gondorian soldiers drink deep and without rationing for the first time in weeks. This is what they defend. This is why the road is worth walking. [Rations: Surplus]

The provision carts overflow with Pelennor wine. Steward or King, the men of Gondor eat and drink as those who know their cause is worth it — and tonight, that knowledge is easy to hold. [Rations: Surplus]
The dungeons overflow. So many captives slow the march and weigh on Gondorian conscience — Steward Denethor demands they be judged swiftly. [Prisoner Burden -3]
Too many captives trail the column. Gondor is not a nation of gaolers — these numbers dishonour the march and test every man's patience. [Prisoner Burden -3]
The column is burdened. Boromir would have said to push them harder; Faramir would say to process them fairly. Both would agree this many prisoners cannot continue. [Prisoner Burden -3]
A handful of prisoners march in the column's wake — enough to process, not enough to slow us. Gondor keeps its order.
The captives are accounted for and moving. Gondor's men manage the column with the same precision they bring to the garrison rosters.
Prisoners are in hand, chains are secured, the march continues. Gondor does not linger over what is already managed.
Few captives drag behind the column. We fight clean — as the sons of Númenor always have. The men's step is lighter for it. [Captive Spoils +3]
No chains slow the Gondorian march today. The White Tree stands for justice, and a column that carries none of war's worst burdens walks in its shadow with pride. [Captive Spoils +3]
The column is clean and quick. Gondor fights for the living, not the imprisoned — and today, the distinction is felt in every stride. [Captive Spoils +3]

The vintage flows and the column marches clean. Gondor at the height of autumn — wine in the cups, honour in the ranks, and the White City waiting at the road's end. This is what we fight for. [Faction Peak]
Lebennin wine and unencumbered soldiers — the Steward's armies at their finest. The Tower of Guard has seen worse days than this, and today is not one of them. [Faction Peak]
Gondor marches as it was made to march: well-provisioned, unburdened, and purposeful. The Men of the West are what they have always been. [Faction Peak]
The wine jars are nearly empty and the dungeons overflow with mouths to feed. Gondor strains under the weight of its own mercy — the men are neither fed nor free in spirit. [Faction Dire]
No wine, too many captives, and a road that doesn't shorten. Gondor has endured sieges and shadow — but this particular combination of privation wears on even the stonest soldier. [Faction Dire]
The cellars are dry and the chains are heavy. The sons of Númenor were not built for this kind of suffering, but they are enduring it anyway. That is all that can be said. [Faction Dire]
Spring comes to Gondor and the road opens. The armies of the White City begin to move after the long winter vigil — there is purpose in every step now.
The fields of the Pelennor are greening. Gondorian soldiers breathe different air in spring — it smells of renewal, of things that could not be taken from them even by shadow.
Spring thaws the passes and opens the marching roads. Gondor's captains are planning; the men are ready. The White Tree buds early this year.
High summer over Gondor and the campaigns are in full motion. The Ithilien patrols ride long and the garrisons stand alert — this is the fighting season, and Gondor knows how to use it.
Midsummer light on the white walls of Minas Tirith, even seen from afar. The men march longer hours and complain less — the long evenings and warm nights make the road bearable.
The summer heat presses on the column but the pace holds. Gondor was built to endure — its soldiers know that summer is not rest; it is when the real work happens.
Autumn in Gondor — the vineyards of Lebennin are at their peak. The harvest is in and the wine is moving. Gondorian soldiers feel the season's generosity even on the march. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

The vintage ripens and the wine-carts roll south. Autumn is Gondor's finest season — the White City smells of pressing grapes and the men in the field can almost taste home. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
The leaves turn gold over the Pelennor and the wine harvest is underway. In autumn, Gondor at war smells like Gondor at peace — and that is the season's gift. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Winter settles over the White Mountains and the patrols grow grimmer. Gondor keeps its vigil through the cold months — the lights of the City burn all the longer for the darkness around them.
Snow on the Ephel Dúath, ice in the mountain passes. The Gondorian column pulls cloaks tight and keeps formation. The White City has never fallen to cold — and it will not start now.
The long winter watch. Gondorian soldiers count their rations, keep their watches, and speak less than usual. Spring will come. It always has.

The vintage runs deep and the march runs clean — this is the third day of Gondor at its finest. The men are beginning to believe in their own legend. The White Tree blooms in every heart. [Sustained Peak]
Days of grace for the sons of Númenor. Wine, honour, and an unburdened road for the third day running. Faramir himself would ride easier knowing the column was in this condition. [Sustained Peak]

Gondor sustains what lesser armies could not. Three days of surplus and clean conscience — the Steward's logistical masterwork is showing. The road ahead looks manageable for the first time in weeks. [Sustained Peak]
The wine has been gone for three days and the dungeons are still overflowing. Gondor bends but does not break — but it is bending. The White Tower feels very far away right now. [Sustained Dire]
This is the third day of the worst of it. Dry cups and burdened columns are not how the sons of Númenor are supposed to march — and the men know it, even if no one says it aloud. [Sustained Dire]
Three days without wine, three days without ease. The Gondorian column presses on because it was built to press on. But something is being spent here that will take time to rebuild. [Sustained Dire]
The grain bags are running thin. Rohirric bread has become Rohirric hardtack, then half-hardtack, then memory. The horses are the last to complain — and even they are quieter.
Last of the Eastfold flour divided before dawn. The Riders of the Mark ride on less than they should, and the horses can feel the tension in the saddle.
Three days since the last full meal. The Rohirrim don't speak of it — they simply ride harder, as if the pace could outrun the hunger. It cannot.
Fresh-milled flour from the golden fields of the Eastfold. The bread of the Riddermark is plain and honest — and the Riders are ready to answer the horn.
Eastfold grain ground before the march, baked on the saddle-stone. Théoden's Riders eat as their fathers ate — simply, quickly, and without complaint.
Bags of Westfold grain divided through the ranks. The Rohirrim do not feast — they fuel. There is a difference, and the difference is the speed of the horse.

The provision wagons are packed with Eastfold grain — more than the campaign needs. The Riders eat well twice over, and the horses are groomed with the patience of men who have nowhere urgent to be. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus harvest from the Riddermark's finest year. Bread is passed freely, seconds are expected, and the Rohirric column rides with the easy speed of an army that has nothing weighing it down. [Rations: Surplus]

The grain sacks are so full they strain the cart-boards. The Riders of the Mark eat like the Riddermark in high harvest — generously, without counting — and the horses run like the wind for it. [Rations: Surplus]
Too many captives slow the column. The Riders of the Mark were not bred to be warders — this many prisoners weigh on Rohirric honour. [Prisoner Burden -3]
The prisoner count has grown past what the column can manage with dignity. Éomer would say: march faster or cut them loose. Neither option is clean. [Prisoner Burden -3]
Chains and captives dragging behind the cavalry — this is not the Rohirrim's way. The horses sense the weight. So do the men. [Prisoner Burden -3]
A few prisoners march behind the column. The Rohirrim keep them moving at a pace that doesn't slow the horse.
Captives in hand, column moving. The Riddermark does not dwell on prisoners when the road is still long.
The prisoner escort is manageable. Rohirric outriders keep them moving — not kindly, not cruelly, just efficiently.
The Riders of the Mark move swift and unencumbered. No chains drag behind the column — only speed and the thunder of hooves. [Captive Spoils +3]
No burden slows the Rohirrim today. The horses feel it first — heads high, strides long, the whole column moving like the open plain. [Captive Spoils +3]
Clean hands and open roads. The Riddermark rides as it was made to ride — fast, free, and unencumbered by what war leaves behind. [Captive Spoils +3]
Saddlebags full of Eastfold grain, and the column rides free as the wind across the Riddermark. The harvest is in and the Mark is unencumbered — Théoden's ghost would approve. [Faction Peak]
Autumn in the Riddermark — grain aplenty and no chains to slow the gallop. The Rohirrim are doing what the Rohirrim do best: riding hard with full bellies. [Faction Peak]
The fields are in and the column is light. Every Rider of the Mark is fed, free, and moving. This is what Helm's Deep was defended for. [Faction Peak]
The grain sacks are nearly empty and too many mouths march in chains behind us. The Riddermark does not starve gracefully — and it does not imprison gracefully either. [Faction Dire]
Half-rations and a column slowed by captives. The Rohirrim are still riding — but they are riding badly, and they know it. [Faction Dire]
Empty grain bags and heavy chains. The horses are restless and the men are hungry. This is not how the Riddermark is supposed to march. [Faction Dire]
Spring comes to the Riddermark and the horses feel it first. Heads higher, strides longer — the Rohirrim trust their mounts' moods, and right now every mount is saying: move.
The Westfold is green and the roads clear. Spring is the season of the Rider — cold enough to ride hard, warm enough to camp without misery. The horn sounds cleaner in spring air.
Snow melts off the Wold and the plains open up. Rohirric outriders ride further and return faster. Something stirs in the blood of the Riddermark when the fields turn green.
High summer on the plains and the grain is growing tall. The Riders keep one eye on the horizon and one on the Eastfold fields — the harvest coming means winter survived. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Midsummer heat on the Riddermark. The horses sweat but they don't slow. Rohirric soldiers were made for exactly this — long light, fast roads, and grain in every pack. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

The great plains bake in summer sun and the grain stands gold to the horizon. The Riders of the Mark know what this season means — abundance coming, campaign season at its peak. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Autumn harvest in the Eastfold — the grain is in. The Rohirrim ride easier knowing the silos are full, even far from home. The horn sounds different after a good harvest.
The Wold turns amber and the stores are counted. Autumn in the Riddermark is a time of reckoning — and this year the reckoning is good.
Harvest home. The fields are empty now, the barns are full, and the Rohirrim can think of war without the second thought of whether the village will eat. That is autumn's gift.
Winter on the Riddermark — the wind comes straight across the plains with nothing to stop it. The Riders huddle closer to the fire and ride closer together. Even horses know to move in winter.
Snow on the White Mountains and cold fog on the Entwash. The Rohirrim endure winter the way they endure everything — without theatrics, without complaint, and ready to ride the moment the ice breaks.
The long winter march. Cold bread and frozen stirrups, but the Riders hold formation. Edoras waits at the other end of winter, warm and lit. That is enough.
The Riddermark sustains what it began — three days of full grain, clean roads, and the thunder of unconstrained hooves. Something legendary is taking shape in the column. [Sustained Peak]
The horses have not flagged in three days. Full grain, no chains, open plains — the Rohirrim are running exactly as Eorl the Young ran them. This is what the Mark was built to be. [Sustained Peak]
Three days of the Riddermark at its absolute finest. The Riders will talk of this march — not loudly, because they are Rohirrim, but they will talk of it. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of thin grain and heavy chains. The horses are restless, the men are quiet, and the column is not moving like itself. The Riddermark bends — but it does not break. Not yet. [Sustained Dire]

This is the third day running. Empty saddlebags and captives slowing the gallop. The Rohirrim endure it because they endure everything — but the cost is being marked somewhere in every rider's eyes. [Sustained Dire]

Three days without what the Mark needs. The column is still moving — but moving like something that knows it shouldn't have to suffer this. The Riddermark deserves better than this march. [Sustained Dire]
The smoke-barrels are empty. The Long Lake fed Dale for a thousand years and now there is no Lake here, only road, and the fish ran out at dawn.
Last of the salt-fish divided in half-portions. The Bardings of Dale are practical to the last — they note the shortage in the ledger and keep walking. But the ledger is marked.
The provision carts are bare. Three days since smoked fish was on the table. The people of Esgaroth know how to go without — they learned it under a dragon — but that does not make it easy.
Lake-fish, smoked over birch embers. The people of Dale have fished the Long Lake since before Smaug darkened the sky — the old taste steadies every heart.
Long Lake trout packed in salt and smoke. King Brand's men carry provisions the way merchants carry goods — practically, efficiently, and without waste.
Barrels of Esgaroth-smoked fish cracked open at midday. The taste is honest and familiar — the same as it was before the dragon, and better for it.

The fish barrels are stacked three high in the provision carts. Dale's quartermaster over-packed — blessedly. The soldiers of Esgaroth eat like the trade-city they came from: well and without apology. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus smoke-fish from a record Long Lake haul. The Bardings distribute seconds and thirds with the matter-of-fact generosity of people who understand supply chains. The march is lighter for it. [Rations: Surplus]

The salt barrels overflow and every soldier carries two days of surplus on their person. King Brand did not rebuild Dale to scrimp on provisions — and today his quartermaster has proved it. [Rations: Surplus]
The column is burdened with captives that slow every decision. Dale's men are merchants and soldiers, not gaolers — this cannot go on. [Prisoner Burden -3]
Too many prisoners for the column to manage cleanly. The Bardings of Dale are practical people — and right now, practically speaking, this is a problem. [Prisoner Burden -3]
Captives outnumber what the escort can process. King Brand did not rebuild Dale to run a prison march. The men's patience is being tested. [Prisoner Burden -3]
A modest number of prisoners walk in the column's wake. The Long Lake folk process them with the same practical efficiency they bring to everything.
Captives accounted for, moving at pace. Dale has always been a city of ledgers — the prisoner column is just another entry in the march's accounts.
The prisoner escort is in hand. Barding soldiers manage it as they manage their market stalls: without sentiment, and without complaint.
Dale's company moves with purpose and clean hands. No burden of captives today — just the road, and men who know why they're on it. [Captive Spoils +3]
No chains slow the column from Esgaroth. The Bardings march light, as befits a people who rebuilt their city from rubble and learned not to carry what they don't need. [Captive Spoils +3]
The march is clean and unencumbered. King Brand's soldiers carry provisions and purpose, nothing more. [Captive Spoils +3]
The spring thaw has filled the nets and the column marches free. Esgaroth smells of smoked fish and fresh possibility — this is what a good march feels like. [Faction Peak]
Spring on the Long Lake and the fish are running. The Bardings carry full barrels and light chains — Dale at its most itself. [Faction Peak]
Full smoke-barrels and an unburdened column. The men from Esgaroth are as content as pragmatic Lake-folk ever get — which is to say, quietly, efficiently satisfied. [Faction Peak]
The fish stocks are low and the prisoners are high. Dale's men are looking at each other with the eyes of people who don't know whether to feed the army or process the captives first. [Faction Dire]
Empty barrels and a column slowed by chains. Dale has survived Smaug — but the dragon at least burned quickly. This marches with you. [Faction Dire]
The smoked fish is gone and the prisoner count is too high. Esgaroth was rebuilt on practicality — and right now, nothing about this march is practical. [Faction Dire]
The Long Lake thaws and the fish begin to run. Spring is Dale's season — the nets go out, the smoke-houses fire up, and the whole city smells of renewal and applewood. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Spring on the shores of the Long Lake: the trout run deep and the Bardings are ready for them. Even on campaign, the smell of spring fish on smoke-wood is a reminder of why Dale was worth rebuilding. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

The ice breaks on Esgaroth's piers and the first boats go out. Spring fish means spring provisions means a well-supplied army — and King Brand's people know how to turn one into the other. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

High summer and the trading roads open fully. Dale is most itself in summer — busy, practical, and moving goods in every direction. The soldiers of Esgaroth march with the energy of people from a city that never really stops.

Midsummer on the Long Lake and the market runs until the small hours. Even on campaign, Dale's soldiers have the alert, transactional energy of a people who cannot fully turn off their trading instincts.
Long summer days on the roads east of Dale. The Bardings trade information with every passing traveler and march with the brisk efficiency of people who know the roads better than anyone.
Autumn in Dale — the last big trade season before winter. The Bardings feel it even on campaign: an urgency, a sense of things being packed away and accounted for before the cold comes.
The Long Lake turns grey in autumn and the last catch comes in. Dale's people preserve and plan — the autumn ledger is the most important of the year, even when there is a war on.
Harvest time in Esgaroth. The soldiers of Dale think of home ledgers and store-rooms being filled. They march with the focused practicality of people who know winter is arithmetic, not poetry.
Winter on the Long Lake — the water darkens and the wind off the Lonely Mountain is merciless. Dale's people have wintered here since before Smaug, and before him too. They know what it costs.

Ice on the Esgaroth piers and snow on the Mountain. The Bardings pull their coats tight and keep walking. Smaug took more from them than cold ever could — and they rebuilt. This, at least, they understand.
The Long Winter descends on the region around Dale. The soldiers march faster in cold — the memory of worse winters lives in Barding bones, and it makes the present one manageable.

Three days of the Long Lake's finest: full smoke-barrels and no chains in the column. The Bardings of Dale are, in their quiet and practical way, thriving. The ledger has never looked better. [Sustained Peak]

Sustained abundance for King Brand's soldiers — fish and freedom for three days running. Dale was rebuilt from ash and dragon-fire. A march this well-provisioned feels like proof it was worth rebuilding. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of Dale at its most itself: practical, well-fed, and unencumbered. The Long Lake people do not make speeches about it — they just keep provisioning at this level and see what happens. [Sustained Peak]
Three days of empty barrels and too many captives. The people of Esgaroth have endured worse — but they remember that 'it could be worse' was also true when Smaug was still alive. [Sustained Dire]
The shortage has held for three days now. Dale's accounting mind has run the numbers: this march is losing ground faster than it is gaining it. Something has to change. [Sustained Dire]

Three days and the situation has not improved. The Bardings of Dale keep marching because that is what they do — but the ledger in every soldier's head shows a column that is deeply in the red. [Sustained Dire]
The lembas pouches are nearly empty. For the Noldor, running out of Elven waybread is not merely a supply problem — it is a sign that something has gone wrong at a deeper level.
Last fragments of lembas distributed among the ranks. The Elves of Rivendell do not complain about hunger — but the absence of the Lady's bread is felt as something more than physical.
The waybread is spent. The Noldor march on as they always march — precisely and without expression — but Imladris has never run dry before, and the fact of it sits heavily on the column.
Elvish waybread, light as parchment and strengthening beyond all mortal measure. The Noldor of Rivendell march as though Valinor itself walks at their heel.
Lembas from Elrond's halls — each bite worth a day's ordinary bread. The Noldor eat with the deliberate gratitude of those who understand exactly what they carry.
Rivendell's waybread passes through the ranks. Even soldiers who have marched for weeks straighten their backs when the lembas arrives — there is something in it beyond sustenance.

The Noldor carry more lembas than any march of this size should need — Elrond's foresight, perhaps, or simply the impossible generosity of Rivendell's kitchens. Each soldier is sustained beyond what was expected. [Rations: Surplus]

The lembas reserves are extraordinary. The Noldor of Imladris march on waybread so plentiful it seems the road itself is fed by Rivendell's grace. The column moves with the ease of the truly, abundantly provisioned. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus waybread from Elrond's storerooms — wrapped in fresh mallorn leaves, each piece more sustaining than the last. The Noldor column is unhurried and unhungered. This is the march of an Elven house at its finest. [Rations: Surplus]
Even the Elves of Rivendell cannot carry this many captives without cost to their spirit. Elrond would counsel mercy or judgment — to linger between them dishonours both. [Prisoner Burden -3]
The column is weighted with prisoners, and Noldor sensibilities are not suited to the work of mass captivity. Elrond's wisdom was never meant for this. [Prisoner Burden -3]
This many captives troubles the Noldor in a way that is difficult to articulate and impossible to ignore. Rivendell is a house of healing. This is not that. [Prisoner Burden -3]
A measured number of prisoners walk in Elven custody. The Noldor are patient wardens — but patience is not the same as comfort.
Prisoners are in hand and the march continues. The Noldor manage the column with precision and a certain weary grace.
The captives walk under Elven watch. Rivendell does not enjoy this work — but Rivendell does not abandon its responsibilities either.
The Noldor march with conscience as clear as the waters of Bruinen — unburdened, swift, and terrible in their beauty. Elrond would approve. [Captive Spoils +3]
No prisoners burden the Noldor column today. The Elves of Imladris move as they were made to move — with perfect grace and no weight that does not need to be carried. [Captive Spoils +3]
The column of Rivendell is clean and swift. Elrond's soldiers carry lembas and purpose — nothing heavier than that is required. [Captive Spoils +3]
Spring in Rivendell — waybread enough to last a lifetime, and no chains to slow the march. The Noldor have never been more themselves than in this moment. [Faction Peak]
The lembas is plentiful and the column marches free. Imladris at its best — serene, purposeful, and carrying nothing that does not belong. [Faction Peak]
Rivendell's finest spring: waybread on every belt and no burden on any conscience. Elrond watches from afar and finds nothing to correct. [Faction Peak]
The waybread is running out and the captives weigh on every Elven heart. Imladris endures worse than this — but not much worse, and not gladly. [Faction Dire]
Empty lembas packs and too many prisoners. The Noldor are enduring — but endurance is not the same as peace, and Rivendell was built for peace. [Faction Dire]
The waybread is spent and the captives number too many. Even the patience of the Eldar has a boundary, and this march is approaching it. [Faction Dire]

Spring in Imladris — the waterfalls run highest and the lembas-making begins anew. The Noldor feel the season in their ancient blood: renewal, the long slow joy of things returning. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

The springs flow full under Rivendell and the waybread is freshly made. Spring lembas carries something of Valinor's light in it — or perhaps that is simply what the Noldor choose to believe, and belief sustains as much as bread. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Elrond's people move through spring with the grace of those who have seen ten thousand of them. The lembas is at its peak and the march is exactly what it should be. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Long summer days in the hidden valley. The Noldor use the long light for council and preparation — summer in Rivendell is not rest but readiness, and the soldiers reflect that in their measured pace.

Midsummer at Imladris: the falls shimmer and the starlight waits patiently for the long days to end. The Noldor march in summer's light with the composure of those who have watched summers come and go since the First Age.
High summer, and the Noldor are at full campaign pace. Long roads, long days, and the precise Elvish efficiency that makes the miles seem shorter than they are.

Autumn comes to Rivendell and the valley turns colours that mortal poets have tried and failed to describe. The Noldor soldiers feel the season's weight of beauty — even on campaign, it is impossible to be entirely unmoved.
The falls of Imladris run slower in autumn. The Noldor prepare for the long season of vigilance — winter in the mountains is the time when shadow moves, and the watchers of Rivendell know this.
Autumn deepens over the Misty Mountains. The Noldor take stock of provisions, reinforce the watches, and move with the focused purpose of people who know what comes after the leaves fall.
Winter in the Misty Mountains and the passes close. Rivendell is never cut off — the Elves find ways the cold cannot reach — but the season demands a different kind of endurance than the others.

Cold has settled on Imladris. The Noldor do not suffer winter the way mortals do, but they feel it as a kind of ancient ache — the memory of the Long Winter in the First Age is not entirely forgotten.

The valley holds against the winter winds. The Noldor keep their watches longer in the cold months, when shadow moves through the passes more freely. The vigil deepens in winter. The soldiers know it.

Three days of lembas abundance and unburdened march. The Noldor of Rivendell have achieved something approaching the ideal of an Elvish campaign — graceful, purposeful, and utterly sufficient. [Sustained Peak]

Imladris sustains this pace with the effortless permanence of an Elvish house that has been doing exactly this for three thousand years. Three days of peak — the Noldor have not noticed the effort. That is the point. [Sustained Peak]
Three days of Rivendell at its most itself. Elrond watching from afar would find nothing to correct and nothing to add. The Noldor march as they were born to march — perfectly. [Sustained Peak]

The third day without lembas and with too many captives. Even the patience of Elrond's people has a limit, and the limit is being approached with the same precise inevitability the Noldor bring to everything. [Sustained Dire]
Three days of this. The Noldor endure because they were made to endure — but endurance was not supposed to be the point of Rivendell. Something fundamental has slipped. [Sustained Dire]
Three consecutive days of Imladris at its worst. The Noldor do not break — they are incapable of it — but something ancient and patient in the column has begun to grieve. [Sustained Dire]
The last Dorwinion barrel tapped three days ago. The wood-elves of Mirkwood do not require wine — but they were designed for beauty, and scarcity is ugly in a way they feel keenly.
The grapes are gone. The Silvan Elves have switched to water from mountain streams — clean, cold, and entirely unsatisfying to those who once drank Dorwinion vintage by moonlight.
Mirkwood's provision carts are empty of the good stuff. The forest-elves march on and make no complaint — but the column is quieter than usual, which for wood-elves means truly, uncomfortably silent.
Barrels of Dorwinion vintage, as the King of Mirkwood would have it. The wood-elves drink deep before they melt back into the trees.
Dorwinion wine, strong and heady, divided with the casual generosity of forest-folk who take pleasure where they find it. Thranduil would have approved this particular cask.
The grapes of Dorwinion — packed in cool barrels and tapped under the canopy. The Silvan Elves drink standing, always with one eye on the treeline.

The provision train carries more Dorwinion vintage than the march could drink in a fortnight. The wood-elves of Mirkwood have, characteristically, brought enough wine for a celebration and a backup celebration. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus casks of Dorwinion — Thranduil's quartermaster was thorough. The Silvan Elves drink well, march well, and move through the forest with the ease of creatures who have never known want in their homeland. [Rations: Surplus]

Overflowing wine barrels in the Mirkwood train. The wood-elves share freely — this much Dorwinion vintage is almost embarrassing, in the best possible way. The forest itself seems pleased. [Rations: Surplus]
Thranduil's halls have served as a prison before — it was not comfortable then, and the company is not comfortable now. Too many captives unsettle even the forest-wise. [Prisoner Burden -3]
The prisoner count has grown beyond what the wood-elves find manageable. Mirkwood keeps its own counsel — and right now, its counsel is that this many captives is too many. [Prisoner Burden -3]
The Silvan Elves are watching the captive column with the wariness they usually reserve for giant spiders. Neither is welcome in their forest. [Prisoner Burden -3]
A few prisoners walk in shadow behind the column. The wood-elves keep one eye on the trees and one on the captives — neither sits entirely easy.
The captives are managed. Mirkwood's soldiers guard them as they guard everything in the forest — silently, efficiently, and with extreme personal space.
Prisoners in hand, march proceeding. The wood-elves do not like this work but they do it — the way they do all unpleasant things, invisibly and without comment.
Mirkwood's warriors move as shadows — swift, unburdened, and lethal. No chains rattle in the column. The wood-elves travel as they were made to travel. [Captive Spoils +3]
The Silvan Elves carry no prisoners today. The column moves like wind through the forest — felt but not seen, and never slowed. [Captive Spoils +3]
No burden trails the wood-elves of Mirkwood. They are as light as they prefer to be, and as swift as they always are. [Captive Spoils +3]
High summer in Mirkwood: the Dorwinion vintage is at its peak, and the column is as free as the forest wind. Even the spiders seem distant today. [Faction Peak]
Summer grapes and an unencumbered march. Thranduil's halls are stocked and his soldiers are free — a rare alignment that puts the whole forest at ease. [Faction Peak]
Dorwinion casks full and no chains in the column. The wood-elves are, in their inscrutable way, content. The great forest breathes a little easier. [Faction Peak]
The Dorwinion barrels are dry and the prisoners outnumber the easy decisions. The wood-elves are resilient, but resilience has a flavour — and right now it tastes of nothing good. [Faction Dire]
Empty wine barrels and a column heavy with captives. Mirkwood has endured darkness before — but usually that darkness doesn't slow the march and drink all the wine first. [Faction Dire]
The vintage is gone and the prisoners are many. The Silvan Elves are looking at each other with the quiet, wide-eyed expression that, in an Elf, means things are genuinely bad. [Faction Dire]

Spring in Mirkwood — the darkness thins and the great spiders retreat to their higher webs. The Silvan Elves move more freely and more joyfully in spring than in any other season. The forest breathes.
The trees of Mirkwood bud in spring and the wood-elves feel it as a physical lifting. The column moves with more ease than it has since winter — light through the canopy, a lighter step below it.
Spring comes to the great forest and the Silvan Elves reclaim their range. Outriders that had pulled back in winter now ride further, and return with news of clear paths and retreating shadows.

High summer in Mirkwood — the great canopy is thick and the forest sounds are alive. The Dorwinion vintage peaks in summer warmth and the wood-elves feel the season in their blood. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Midsummer under the Mirkwood canopy. The grapes ripen in the valley beyond and the Silvan Elves drink in anticipation of what the late-summer casks will bring. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

The forest is at its fullest and the Dorwinion is at its best. Summer in Mirkwood is the season of the wood-elves at their most themselves — alive in every sense the word can hold. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Autumn gold in the Mirkwood canopy. The Silvan Elves move through falling leaves with a grace that makes the season look like it was designed for them — perhaps it was.
The great forest turns in autumn. The wood-elves harvest what the season gives and prepare the watches for the darker months ahead — when shadow moves most freely under bare branches.
Autumn in Mirkwood is beautiful and slightly ominous, which suits the Silvan Elves perfectly. They prepare the winter watches, seal the Dorwinion casks, and wait for whatever the dark months bring.
Winter closes the high paths of Mirkwood and the shadow moves through the leafless trees more easily. The wood-elves tighten their watches and speak less — listening for what winter hides.

The forest goes quiet in winter. The Silvan Elves find it unsettling in a way they cannot explain to mortals — a wood without leaves is not quite a wood, and a wood-elf in such a place is not quite at home.
Cold in the great forest. The Silvan Elves endure winter by becoming more watchful — everything they do not need they shed, and what remains is the essential, patient vigilance of an ancient wood.
Three days of Dorwinion surplus and unburdened forest paths. The wood-elves of Mirkwood are, in their inscrutable way, flourishing — and the great forest seems to know it. [Sustained Peak]

The Silvan Elves have maintained this pace for three days. Casks full, column clean, the forest welcoming rather than threatening. This is what Mirkwood looked like before the shadow came — or so the oldest elves say. [Sustained Peak]
Three days of peak. The Dorwinion is flowing, the march is free, and the wood-elves are moving through the world with the easy mastery of those for whom this was always home. [Sustained Peak]

Three days without vintage and with too many captives. The Silvan Elves are still moving, still watching — but the forest seems to feel their diminished state, and it is quieter than usual. [Sustained Dire]
This is the third day of the worst of Mirkwood's campaign. Dry barrels and heavy chains and a column that moves like it knows it shouldn't have to move like this. [Sustained Dire]

Three days running. The wood-elves endure — they were made to endure a forest full of shadow. But shadow in the supply chain is a different problem, and the column is beginning to show it. [Sustained Dire]
The lembas is nearly spent. The Galadhrim move on in silence — but the absence of the Lady's bread is felt as a dimming, as though a light has gone out somewhere just beyond perception.

Last pieces of waybread counted out carefully among the Galadhrim. The Golden Wood does not practice scarcity — the Lady sees to that — but the march has gone long, and even Lothlórien's grace has limits.

Empty mallorn-leaf wrappings in the provision packs. The lembas is gone and the march continues on ordinary rations. The Galadhrim do not complain. They remember what the waybread felt like and walk toward the memory.
Lembas — the Waybread of the Galadhrim, wrapped in leaves of the mallorn. One bite fills the stomach of a grown warrior. The Lady's gift sustains beyond all else.
Galadriel's lembas, each piece a marvel of Elvish craft. The soldiers of Lothlórien eat sparingly and deliberately — to waste even a crumb would be to dishonour the gift.
Mallorn-leaf wrapped waybread passed through the ranks in reverent silence. The Galadhrim know what the lembas costs to make. They eat accordingly.

The Galadhrim carry more lembas than any march should need — the Lady was generous, or foreseeing, or both. The column moves with the easy grace of those who are not rationing hope. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus waybread from the Golden Wood — each soldier carries enough for a week, wrapped in fresh mallorn leaves that keep the bread as though it were just made. The Lady's provision extends further than the road. [Rations: Surplus]

The lembas supply is extraordinary. The Galadhrim march on Lothlórien's finest — sustained, serene, and sustained further still. This is what it means to carry the Golden Wood's blessing into the world. [Rations: Surplus]
Even the Golden Wood cannot remain untouched by so many captives. The Lady watches from afar and is saddened — such weight does not belong on the Galadhrim. [Prisoner Burden -3]
The prisoner column is too long for Lothlorien's conscience. The Galadhrim are not without steel — but they are not without mercy either, and right now mercy is losing. [Prisoner Burden -3]
This many captives darkens the spirit of the march. Galadriel's mirror shows many things — and none of them look like this. [Prisoner Burden -3]
A small number of prisoners walk in the company's care. The Galadhrim attend to them as they attend to all things — with grace and an undercurrent of sadness.
Captives in hand, column moving. The Galadhrim guard them without cruelty and without sentiment — as the Lady would have it.
The prisoners are managed. Lothlorien does not enjoy captivity as a condition of war — but it accepts it as a consequence.
The Galadhrim carry no chains today. They move as the Lady moves — with grace, purpose, and a terrible, serene beauty. The Golden Wood does not weigh itself down. [Captive Spoils +3]
No prisoners burden the soldiers of Lothlórien. The column moves as light as mallorn blossom — Galadriel's soldiers at their most themselves. [Captive Spoils +3]
The march is unburdened. The Galadhrim carry only what they carry — and what they carry is purpose, lembas, and the light of the Lady's blessing. [Captive Spoils +3]
The mallorn trees are in bloom and the lembas is plentiful. No chains drag behind the column. The Golden Wood has never felt more like itself — and neither has this company. [Faction Peak]
Spring under the mallorn canopy: lembas stocked, column free, the Lady's light on every face. Lothlorien at its most radiant. [Faction Peak]
The Golden Wood gives its best: full waybread packs and an unburdened march. The Galadhrim are, in this moment, exactly what they are meant to be. [Faction Peak]

The lembas is nearly spent and the captives are many. Even Galadriel's light has limits when it is stretched this thin. The Galadhrim march forward because they always do — but the weight is real. [Faction Dire]
Empty lembas pouches and too many chains. The Golden Wood sends its soldiers out to uphold the light — and right now, the light is doing poorly. [Faction Dire]
The Lady's waybread is gone and the prisoner column lengthens. Lothlorien does not break easily — but it does not pretend this isn't breaking something. [Faction Dire]

Spring comes to the Golden Wood and the mallorn trees burst into flower. The Galadhrim feel the season as a renewal that goes deeper than warmth — it is a reopening, the world becoming itself again. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

The mallorn flowers fall like golden snow on the spring marches of the Galadhrim. The lembas is freshly made and the Lady's power is nearest in spring — the column moves in its light. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Spring in Lothlórien: the greatest season. The waybread is made fresh, the mallorn is in flower, and the Galadhrim march with the unhurried certainty of those who know exactly what they carry. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Summer in the Golden Wood — the mallorn canopy is thick and golden-green and the Lady's mirror reflects long bright days. The Galadhrim move through summer with the serenity of the ageless.
High summer and the Golden Wood is at its most opulent. The Galadhrim soldiers walk paths that have been walked since the First Age — even in war, the beauty of their homeland travels with them.

Midsummer light in Lothlórien. The Galadhrim campaign in summer with the same grace they bring to everything — efficiently, without haste, and never losing sight of why the Golden Wood must be protected.
The mallorn trees turn gold in autumn — a second flowering, almost. The Galadhrim feel the season's beauty as a kind of bittersweet ache. Even the Lady seems more present in autumn light.

Autumn in the Golden Wood is a season of quiet preparation. The Galadhrim seal the waybread, reinforce the flets, and take stock with the unhurried thoroughness of people who have prepared for many winters.

Gold leaves from golden trees, falling in Lothlórien's autumn. The Galadhrim march through the season with the awareness that beauty is not permanent — and the determination that certain things should be.

Winter brings a different quality of silence to the Golden Wood — deeper and more present than the usual Elven quiet. The Galadhrim hold their watches with extra attention in winter. The Lady watches too.

Cold deepens around Lothlórien but the mallorn trees do not lose their leaves in winter — they hold their gold against the grey season. The Galadhrim find this a comfort. Not everything must yield to cold.
The winter watches of Lothlórien. The Galadhrim move through the cold months with the same serene precision as the warm ones — but the precision is sharper now, and the eyes never quite rest.

Three days of the Golden Wood at its most radiant. Lembas abundant, march unburdened, the Lady's blessing palpable in every step. The Galadhrim are, in this moment, the best version of what they were made to be. [Sustained Peak]

The Galadhrim have sustained this for three days. Lothlórien's finest provision and cleanest march, held without effort. The Lady sees this and approves — and her approval is a thing the column can feel. [Sustained Peak]
Three days of peak in the Golden Wood's service. The mallorn light travels with the soldiers even far from home. This is what Galadriel sent them out to be. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of this. The lembas is spent, the captives are many, and even the Galadhrim's centuries of composure are showing hairline fractures. The Golden Wood's soldiers endure — but endurance has never been the point here. [Sustained Dire]

The third day running. The Lady's soldiers were not made for this kind of sustained hardship, and the fact that they are bearing it perfectly does not mean it isn't costing them something irreplaceable. [Sustained Dire]

Three consecutive days at the furthest point from everything Lothlórien stands for. The Galadhrim march on. But the light in their eyes has dimmed by exactly the degree that three days of this should dim it. [Sustained Dire]
The Cram is gone. The Dwarves of Erebor don't bother to announce it — they simply eat less and march harder, which is what Dwarves have always done when the stores run low.

Last blocks of Cram rationed at half-portion. The sons of Durin have mined through mountain crises before — a supply shortage is merely a different kind of obstacle, and they will excavate through it.
The provision carts are empty of Cram and the column marches on determination. Dwarves fed on stubbornness alone have moved mountains. This is merely a road.
Cram — the iron ration of the Dwarves of the Lonely Mountain. Hard, dense, and utterly without flavour. Under Erebor it has fuelled a thousand impossible things.
Erebor's Cram divided through the ranks without ceremony. Dwarves do not make food an occasion — they make it fuel, and fuel is what this is.
Blocks of Dwarven Cram passed hand to hand. Thorin's heirs did not rebuild the Lonely Mountain on fine cuisine — they rebuilt it on exactly this, and it was enough.

The provision wagons are overloaded with Cram — Erebor's quartermaster packed for a siege, not a march. The Dwarves eat double and still have surplus. The mountain provides, even in the field. [Rations: Surplus]

More Cram than the column can consume in a fortnight. The sons of Durin carry it without complaint — Dwarves are accustomed to bearing heavy loads — and eat with the focused efficiency of creatures who treat surplus as a professional responsibility. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus Cram from the deep stores of the Lonely Mountain. The Dwarves are eating well by any standard and uncommonly well by Dwarven standards. The march is fuelled beyond what was planned, and the pace reflects it. [Rations: Surplus]
Dwarven halls are not dungeons for the softer races. Too many prisoners slow the company and trouble the Dwarves' practical sensibilities. [Prisoner Burden -3]
The captive count is too high for the Erebor column to manage efficiently. Dwarves are miners and warriors, not prison wardens — and the distinction is starting to show. [Prisoner Burden -3]
Too many prisoners weigh on a march that was never designed for this. The sons of Durin grumble — and a grumbling Dwarf is a Dwarf whose axe arm is getting restless. [Prisoner Burden -3]
A handful of prisoners are being managed with the grim efficiency the Dwarves bring to all administrative matters. It is not pleasant, but it is organised.
The captives are in custody and the march proceeds. Erebor handles its prisoner column the way it handles ore extraction — by the numbers, without sentiment.
Prisoners accounted for. The Dwarves of Erebor note it in their ledgers and move on. There are bigger mountains to excavate.
No prisoners slow the Dwarves of Erebor. The company marches with the relentless weight of the mountain itself — and none of that weight is chains. [Captive Spoils +3]
The Dwarven column carries no burden of captives today. Just Cram, axes, and the particular forward momentum of a people who do not stop for much. [Captive Spoils +3]
No chains. No delays. Erebor's soldiers march the way Dwarves always march — like the mountain is already behind them and the next one is already in sight. [Captive Spoils +3]
Deep winter, and the Cram stores are full. No prisoners slow the column. The Dwarves of Erebor in their element — cold, purposeful, and completely unstoppable. [Faction Peak]
Winter beneath the Lonely Mountain: Cram aplenty and no burden on the march. The sons of Durin are at their best when the cold is deep and the road is clear. [Faction Peak]
Full Cram packs, unburdened soldiers, deep winter. Dwarves were made for this. Every step says so. [Faction Peak]
The Cram is nearly gone and the prisoner count is climbing. Even Dwarven stubbornness has a breaking point — and right now the march is testing it. [Faction Dire]
Empty Cram packs and too many captives in the column. Erebor has been besieged by dragons. This is different — more inconvenient, somehow, and longer. [Faction Dire]
The rations are spent and the chains are heavy. Dwarves endure — but enduring hungry with too many prisoners is a particular kind of misery even the sons of Durin find hard to ignore. [Faction Dire]

Spring thaws the mountain passes and the Dwarves resume their expeditions. The sons of Erebor feel spring as a reopening — halls connect to the world again, and the world has things Dwarves want from it.
Ice breaks in the mountain streams and the Erebor column moves out of winter quarters. Spring is the season of ambitious plans and renewed digging schedules. The Dwarves have both ready.
The high passes clear in spring and the Lonely Mountain opens fully to the outside world. Erebor's merchants are already calculating the trading season. The soldiers note it with approval.

Midsummer and the surface world swelters. The Dwarves of Erebor march through the heat with the patient endurance of people who spend most of their time underground — outside weather is a temporary inconvenience.

High summer on the roads from the Lonely Mountain. The sun is merciless but the Dwarves are more so. Thorin's heirs were not made comfortable by their years in reclamation, and they do not start being comfortable now.
The summer roads are long and hot and the Dwarves of Erebor walk them anyway. Deep in the mountain, it is always cool. The soldiers hold that thought and keep moving.

Autumn on the approaches to Erebor — the first chill from the mountain reminds the Dwarves of home. The harvest season means the stores are being filled, and the Lonely Mountain is at its most comfortable in a stocked autumn.
The mountain air turns cold in autumn and the Dwarves of Erebor are glad for it. The cold reminds them of the deep halls. The deep halls remind them of why they marched.

Autumn provisions are being packed into the deep stores of Erebor. The soldiers on campaign know this even far from home — the mountain is being stocked, and they will return to a full larder. It is a comfort.

Deep winter and the Lonely Mountain is sealed against the cold. The Dwarves of Erebor are most themselves in winter — inside, purposeful, warm in the deep halls with the mountain above them. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Winter is Erebor's season. The stores are full, the forges burn, and the outer world is held at bay by stone and season. The soldiers campaign in conditions that feel almost like home. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Snow on the Mountain, warmth in the deep halls, Cram in the packs. Winter is when Erebor truly belongs to the Dwarves — and their soldiers march with the confidence of people on familiar ground. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Three days of Erebor at its absolute finest — deep winter, full stores, no burden on the march. The Dwarves of the Lonely Mountain are doing exactly what they were built to do: endure, persist, and prevail. [Sustained Peak]

The sons of Durin have sustained this for three days. Full Cram, clean march, deep cold. Something has clicked into place in the Erebor column that Thorin himself would have recognised as right. [Sustained Peak]

Three consecutive days of the Lonely Mountain's finest. The Dwarves are in their element and they know it — which, for creatures of absolute practicality, is the closest thing they have to joy. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of running low. The Dwarves of Erebor have faced worse — they retook a mountain from a dragon — but that does not make three days of empty Cram packs and heavy prisoner escort any easier to account for. [Sustained Dire]

The third day of the worst stretch. Dwarven stubbornness is not infinite — it is very, very large, but it has a floor, and three days of this has brought the column closer to that floor than it has been in a long time. [Sustained Dire]

Three days and still no improvement. The sons of Durin endure because that is what they do. But something in the deep Dwarven accounting of worth and cost has recorded this stretch, and the record will not be kind. [Sustained Dire]

The root-scrape is gone. The Dunlendings pick at bark and bitter herb and call it a meal. They have eaten worse — the hills gave them worse for generations — but the grudge is an old one, and hunger sharpens it.

Nothing in the provision sacks but grit and memory. The hill-folk of Dunland were never well-fed — it was one of their grievances against the valley people — and right now that grievance feels very specific.
The food is gone. The wild-men of the Westmarch eat what the hills give and the hills, today, give nothing. The column marches on emptiness and the oldest fuel the Dunlendings know: resentment.
Root and bitter herb scraped from the Dunland hills. The hill-folk have always made do with little — they ride no less fiercely for eating plain.
Dunland roots and dried hill-plants, passed around without ceremony. The wild-men of the Westmarch do not eat for pleasure — they eat to continue.
Bitter hill-scrape divided through the war-band. The Dunlendings have lived on grudge and root-vegetable for generations. Both still serve.

The provision carts carry more than the Dunlendings expected — traded or seized, it doesn't matter which. For hill-folk who have gone without most of their lives, an abundance of even bitter roots is worth marking. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus provisions in a Dunland column — rare enough to warrant a second glance. The wild-men of the Westmarch eat with the focused intensity of people who have learned never to waste what they have, since they never had much. [Rations: Surplus]
More root and herb than the column needs for once. The hill-folk eat well by their standards — which is to say, they have enough, which is more than they usually count on. [Rations: Surplus]
The Dunlending column is slowed by captives it has no use for. Hill-folk keep little they cannot sell or release — and this many prisoners is just slowing everything down.
Too many prisoners for the hill-men's patience. Dunlending war-bands travel light and move fast — and right now they are moving neither.
The captive count has grown to the point where even the hill-chieftains are questioning it. Dunlendings do not prison-march well. This much is becoming obvious.
A modest number of prisoners keep pace behind the column. The Dunlendings watch them with the casual suspicion they direct at most things.
Captives are in hand. The hill-folk manage them the same way they manage everything — brusquely, without explanation, and without particular care.
The prisoners are being moved. Dunlending war-bands do not have established protocols for this — but they are improvising, which is what they always do.
The hill-folk travel light — no prisoners, no surplus, no sentiment. Dunlending war-bands move fast and fade into the hills like they were never there.
No captives slow the Dunlendings today. The hill-men move as they always preferred to move — quickly, quietly, and without witnesses.
Empty chains, fast march. The wild-men of the Westmarch are doing what they do best: moving through difficult country without anything dragging them down.
Summer in Dunland: the root crops are good and the column travels unencumbered. The hill-folk are as content as they ever get — which is to say: suspicious, but fed.
Dunland summer, root harvest in, column moving clean. This is as close to prosperity as the hill-folk know — and they will not waste it on gratitude.
Vegetables aplenty and no burden of chains. The Dunlendings have had worse seasons — most of them, in fact. This one is, by their standards, almost good.
Bitter hill scraps and too many captives to feed. The Dunlendings are not a people known for restraint under pressure — and pressure is building.
Empty hillside scratchings and a column slowed by prisoners. The wild-men of Dunland are hungry and irritable — a combination that has never ended well for anyone nearby.
The roots are gone and the captives are too many. Dunlending war-bands in this state typically resolve their problems simply and decisively. That is not necessarily reassuring.
Spring in Dunland — the grievances thaw before the ground does. The hill-folk begin to move again after the winter's frozen fury, and movement always leads toward the valley people, sooner or later.
The hills green up in spring and the Dunlending war-bands come down from their winter shelters. The hill-folk are suspicious of spring, as they are suspicious of everything — but they use it.
Spring thaw in the Westmarch. The wild-men of Dunland take stock of what winter took from them and begin the annual process of deciding what they are owed. The answer is always: more than they have.

High summer in the Dunland hills — the root crops are coming in and the long days make everything seem more possible than it is. The hill-folk are briefly, cautiously almost optimistic. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Midsummer and the Dunlending harvest is building. The wild-men of the Westmarch eat slightly better in summer than any other season, and slightly better is, for them, a meaningful improvement. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Summer in the hills. The roots and herbs are at their peak and the war-bands are moving with the confidence of people who, for once, are not going hungry. The column marches harder on a full stomach. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Autumn in Dunland — the harvest is in and the hill-folk are already calculating how long it will last. The answer, as always, is not long enough. The winter grudge begins to build in autumn.
The root stores are packed and the Dunlendings begin to watch the sky. Autumn in the Westmarch is the season of 'this will have to do' — practical, grim, and slightly less bitter than winter.
Autumn wind in the hills. The wild-men of Dunland hoard what the season gave them and prepare for what the cold will take. They have always been good at preparing for loss.

Deep winter in the Dunland hills and the cold is the hill-folk's oldest companion. They were born in the cold, raised on the cold, and the cold has made them something the valley people never quite understand: durable.
Snow on the Westmarch and the Dunlendings huddle together with the unsentimental solidarity of people who have survived too many winters to be surprised by this one.
The worst of the winter cold. The hill-folk eat what they stored in autumn, sleep as close to the fire as is survivable, and wait. They are very good at waiting. They have had a lot of practice.

Three days of summer abundance — full roots and an unencumbered march. For the Dunlendings, this much good fortune in a row is almost suspicious. They keep moving and try not to examine it too closely. [Sustained Peak]

The wild-men of Dunland have had three days of the best conditions they've seen in this campaign. They are not celebrating — celebrating invites the attention of things that take good fortune away. They just keep moving. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of Dunland at its accidental best. The hill-folk are fed, unencumbered, and moving well. Something is going right, and the Dunlendings are grimly determined to run through it before it ends. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of hunger and captives and impossible roads. The Dunlendings have endured this their entire lives — but knowing something is survivable doesn't make surviving it feel any different. [Sustained Dire]
The third day. The hill-folk are running on the oldest Dunlending fuel: pure, accumulated grievance. It has always been enough before. They trust it will be enough now. [Sustained Dire]
Three days and the column has not improved. The wild-men of the Westmarch march forward because going back is not an option. It has never been an option. The hills taught them that. [Sustained Dire]

The meat is gone. Mordor's soldiers do not complain — complaining requires the expectation of better, and the servants of the Dark Lord have no such expectation. But the march is slower, and the Eye notices.
Empty ration racks. The column moves forward on Sauron's will and nothing else. The Dark Lord's servants have been fed on shadow and terror before — it keeps them moving, if not satisfied.

No meat for three days. The Orcs are getting that look — the one that precedes either a very good ambush or a very bad incident within the column itself. Either way, something is going to be consumed.
Meat's back on the menu, boys.
The rations are raw and the soldiers don't care. Mordor feeds its own on conquest — and today, there is enough conquest for everyone.
Fresh kill divided without asking what it was. The soldiers of the Dark Lord eat as they fight — quickly, without sentiment, and ready to do it again.

The meat racks are overflowing. Mordor's soldiers eat until they cannot, then are told to eat more. The Dark Lord does not waste resources — surplus is pre-positioned conquest, and the Orcs are filling out accordingly. [Rations: Surplus]

More meat than the column can consume. Sauron's quartermaster overshot the supply calculation and nobody is complaining. The Orcs of Mordor in a genuine surplus are a terrifying thing — fat with confidence and hunger. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus in the ranks of Mordor — the kill was exceptional and the cages were restocked before the march. The Eye looks on what it has wrought and finds it, for once, adequately provisioned. [Rations: Surplus]
Fresh slaves fuel the Dark Lord's war machine. The pits of Mordor will be well-stocked this season — Sauron is pleased, and his displeasure falls elsewhere tonight. [Captive Spoils +5]
The cages are full. Sauron's industry never sleeps and tonight it feeds well. The soldiers of Mordor march harder when they know the pits are being stocked. [Captive Spoils +5]
Prisoners enough to satisfy the Eye for now. The Dark Lord does not celebrate — but he does not punish either, which amounts to the same thing in Mordor. [Captive Spoils +5]
A steady trickle of prisoners flows into Mordor's keeping. Not enough to feast on, but enough to keep the machinery of the Dark Lord turning. [Prisoners in Column +2]
Captives enough to meet the quota. The Eye is neither pleased nor displeased — and in Mordor, neutrality is its own kind of relief. [Prisoners in Column +2]
The prisoner column moves. Sauron's servants have learned to find comfort in adequate performance. Excellence is dangerous; so is failure. Adequate is safe. [Prisoners in Column +2]
Sauron demands fresh slaves for the pits — and you have brought him none. The Dark Lord's patience is not infinite, and his displeasure is already felt in the ranks. [Prisoner Burden -5]
Empty chains. The Eye is watching and finding the tally insufficient. In Mordor, the cost of failure is not abstract — it is immediate and personal. [Prisoner Burden -5]
The pits stand empty and the Dark Lord is displeased. His displeasure travels through the ranks like cold smoke, and it settles on every soldier who can feel it. [Prisoner Burden -5]

The racks are groaning with meat, the cages overflow with fresh captives, and winter has settled over Mordor like a blessing. Sauron's Eye is fixed elsewhere — the servants of the Dark Lord march in something resembling joy. [Faction Peak]

Full meat racks, full cages, cold winter. Everything the servants of Sauron need is present in abundance. The Eye looks on with something that might, in another creature, be called approval. [Faction Peak]
Winter in Mordor at its best: meat for the ranks and slaves for the pits. The Dark Lord's servants have everything they need and the campaign is proceeding as he intends. [Faction Peak]

The meat is gone and the pits stand empty. Cold ash and empty chains — the worst possible state for the servants of the Dark Lord. Even the Nazgul seem more ominous when the Eye turns inward with disappointment. [Faction Dire]
No meat. No prisoners. The Eye of Sauron is watching and finding nothing to approve of. In Mordor, a general in this position does not remain a general long. [Faction Dire]
Empty racks and empty cages in deep winter. This is Mordor at its worst — not because the cold is bad, but because the Dark Lord knows, and he is waiting. [Faction Dire]

Spring thaws the plains around Mordor and the Ash Mountains breathe cold air into the lowlands. Sauron's armies move more freely as the ice breaks — the Eye looks outward with the focused attention of a new campaign season.

The Eye turns west in spring. Mordor's armies adjust to the roads clearing and the passes opening — more movement means more opportunity, and opportunity is what the servants of the Dark Lord are built to exploit.
Spring comes to the Black Land in its thin, grudging way. The ground is less frozen, the passes less blocked, and the campaign season opens with the grinding inevitability of Sauron's long plans.
Summer in Mordor — the volcanic heat adds to the season's warmth in ways that make the Black Land nearly uninhabitable for anything with normal body temperature. The Orcs are largely fine with this.
High summer and Mordor is at its most itself: hot, dark, and relentless. The Eye surveys the surrounding lands and finds the campaign opportunities multiplying as the roads dry.

Midsummer under the shadow of the Ash Mountains. The heat is extraordinary and the soldiers of the Dark Lord march through it with the blunt persistence of things that were never designed to be comfortable.
Autumn shadow deepens over Mordor — the dark comes earlier and the Eye is more present in the long evenings. The soldiers feel Sauron's attention most sharply in autumn's lengthening nights.

The season turns and the shadow stretches further from the Black Gate. Autumn in Mordor is the season of gathering — the armies consolidate, the stores are filled, and the Eye prepares for winter's campaigns.

Dark autumn in the shadow of Doom. The servants of Sauron feel the season's change as a deepening of their purpose — darker days mean more familiar darkness, and Mordor's soldiers are creatures of the dark.

Deep winter in Mordor — cold and ash and the grinding permanence of the Eye's gaze. This is what the servants of the Dark Lord were built for. The shadow is thickest in winter. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Winter over the Black Land. Mordor's armies march through the cold with the absolute certainty of those who have never needed warmth to keep moving. The Eye burns through the snow unchanged. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

The coldest season and the Dark Lord's favourite. The lands around Mordor are at their most vulnerable in winter — the passes icy, the defenders cold, and the servants of Sauron entirely at home in it. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Three days of the Dark Lord's finest — full meat racks, full cages, winter cold. Sauron's servants are at peak operational capacity, and the Eye has found nothing to punish for three consecutive days. That itself is extraordinary. [Sustained Peak]

The servants of Mordor have sustained this for three days. Meat and prisoners and winter cold and the Eye's distant but tangible approval. This is as good as it gets in the shadow's service. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of Mordor operating exactly as designed. The Dark Lord does not celebrate — but the absence of his displeasure for three full days is the closest thing his servants will ever know to a holiday. [Sustained Peak]

Three days without meat, three days with empty cages. The Eye has been watching this column for three consecutive days of underperformance. The servants of the Dark Lord do not have the luxury of hope. They have only the deadline. [Sustained Dire]

The third day of Sauron's displeasure. The servants of Mordor have survived worse — they were built to survive worse — but the Eye does not value survival. It values delivery. And the delivery has failed for three days. [Sustained Dire]

Three days running and the numbers haven't improved. Whatever is left of the column's morale is being sustained entirely by the knowledge that the alternative to continuing is something worse than continuing. [Sustained Dire]
The ration carts are empty. Saruman's Uruks do not understand hunger as complaint — they understand it as malfunction. The column is malfunctioning and the White Wizard is calculating corrections.

No meat in the column for three days. The Uruk-hai are beginning to look at each other with the specific assessment of creatures for whom everything is potentially a resource. Someone needs to resupply soon.
Empty racks. The industrial army of Isengard was built on throughput, and right now the throughput has stopped. Saruman's creation is running on momentum and nothing else.
Raw flesh is divided through the ranks without ceremony. The Uruk-hai do not slow to cook — they eat as they march and they kill as they breathe.
Isengard's soldiers eat their kill without fire. Saruman bred them to move fast and need little — and that is what they are doing.
Meat torn and distributed on the march. The Uruks of Isengard were made in pits and fed on the go — they have no other relationship with food, and want none.

The kill was exceptional and the racks are overloaded. Isengard's Uruks eat beyond capacity and march faster for it — Saruman bred creatures who convert fuel to speed with terrifying efficiency. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus meat in the White Hand's column — more than the march needs, less than the Uruk-hai would choose to consume. They eat it all anyway. Saruman didn't breed restraint into them. [Rations: Surplus]

The ration wagons are overloaded and the Uruk-hai are eating with the focused brutality of creatures for whom surplus is simply an instruction to move faster. Isengard at surplus is a frightening thing. [Rations: Surplus]
Saruman's pits are fed. Hands for the forge, backs for the tunnels — the White Hand's industry never sleeps. The Uruk-hai march harder for knowing the forges are full. [Captive Spoils +5]
The cages are full and Isengard's productivity is at its peak. Saruman does not praise — but the Uruks know a well-stocked pit when they see one. [Captive Spoils +5]
Full cages means full forges means more Uruks means more campaigns. Isengard's industrial logic is brutal but functional, and today it is functioning at capacity. [Captive Spoils +5]
A working number of prisoners are being fed into Saruman's operation. Isengard is efficient — not glorious, but efficient. [Prisoners in Column +2]
The prisoner tally is acceptable. Saruman's machinery requires constant feeding, and currently it is being fed at a sustainable rate. [Prisoners in Column +2]
Captives moving toward the forges. Isengard keeps no prisoners for sentiment — only for utility. And utility is currently being served. [Prisoners in Column +2]
Saruman's pits stand empty and the forges are short of hands. The Uruk-hai need something to fight for beyond orders — right now, there's nothing to show for the march. [Prisoner Burden -5]
Empty pits and cold forges. Saruman's production depends on a steady supply, and the supply has stopped. The Wizard is not pleased. [Prisoner Burden -5]
The forges are idle and the pits are empty. Isengard without industry is just a tower — and towers do not win wars. The Uruks are feeling the emptiness. [Prisoner Burden -5]

Cold winter, full cages, and raw meat in the ranks. Saruman's industrial nightmare is running at peak efficiency — the Uruks are as close to satisfied as their creator ever intended them to be. [Faction Peak]
Isengard at maximum capacity: full meat rations, full prisoner intake, forges burning. Saruman watches the numbers and finds nothing to correct. [Faction Peak]
The White Hand's operation is running exactly as designed. Fed Uruks, full cages, deep winter. If Saruman could smile without it meaning something terrible, this would be the moment. [Faction Peak]

Empty pits and empty mouths. Isengard was built on production and the production has stopped. The forges are cold and the Uruk-hai are looking at each other in a way that only ends one way. [Faction Dire]
No meat, no prisoners, no production. Saruman's system requires all three, and currently has none of them. The White Wizard is somewhere recalculating. [Faction Dire]

The industrial machinery of Isengard has ground to a halt. Empty racks, idle forges, cold pits. Orthanc has seen setbacks before — but those setbacks had the courtesy to come from outside. [Faction Dire]
Spring thaws the plains and opens the roads from Isengard. Saruman's operations expand in spring — new routes, new targets, new intake for the pits. The White Hand reaches further as the roads clear.

The Isen swells in spring and the Uruks march over it without ceremony. Spring means more territory accessible, which means more everything else. Isengard's expansion is a function of season as much as strategy.
Spring comes to the Wizard's Vale and the forges restart from winter maintenance. The Uruks feel the season as an acceleration — more output, more range, more of what Saruman demands.
High summer and the forges of Isengard run day and night. The Uruk-hai are at their most productive in summer — heat doesn't bother creatures who were bred in volcanic pits.
Midsummer in the Wizard's Vale. The production numbers are good and the Uruk columns are moving at maximum range. Saruman reviews his maps and finds reasons to be almost satisfied.
Summer heat and the forges never stop. Isengard's industrial momentum is at its seasonal peak — the Uruk-hai march harder in summer as though the heat itself is a catalyst for whatever drives them.
Autumn in Isengard — the trees around the Wizard's Vale are being cut for fuel and lumber. Saruman looks at the rings and sees timber; the Ents, further off, notice something else entirely.
The cold approaches and Isengard's forges are adjusted for winter capacity. The Uruks continue their operations with the indifference to season of creatures born in a hole in the ground.
Autumn in the Wizard's Vale and the great wheel turns. Isengard's production adjusts, the Uruk-hai numbers are updated, and Saruman's plans proceed with their usual terrifying logic.

Deep winter and the forges of Isengard glow through the snow. The Uruk-hai were bred to function in any condition — and they do. Saruman looks at the output and finds it adequate. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Winter in the Wizard's Vale. The cold doesn't slow Isengard's operations — the pits are warm and the Uruks were never built for comfort anyway. The White Hand is coldest in winter, which makes it most itself. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Snow on the Iron Ring but fire in the forges. Isengard at winter is exactly what it is in summer — producing, expanding, consuming. The season is irrelevant to Saruman's mathematics. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Three days of Isengard at maximum capacity: full racks, full cages, winter cold. The White Hand is producing at a rate Saruman can actually approve of. Three consecutive days of adequate results in Isengard is a streak. [Sustained Peak]

The White Hand's operation has sustained peak efficiency for three days. The Uruk-hai are fed, the pits are full, and Saruman's calculations show a surplus. This is what the breeding was for. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of Isengard running as designed. The forges are hot, the intake is good, and the Uruk columns are moving at full stride. Saruman reviews the reports and something in his face almost relaxes. Almost. [Sustained Peak]

Three consecutive days of underperformance. Saruman's industrial logic does not accommodate excuses — three days of empty racks and empty pits means three days of lost production, and lost production means lost war. [Sustained Dire]

The third day running. The Uruk-hai are still moving but they are moving with the specific aggression of creatures whose fuel has run out. Saruman is somewhere rearranging his calculations. [Sustained Dire]

Three days and no improvement. Isengard's operation has a minimum viable throughput, and this march has been below it for three consecutive days. The White Wizard is not forgiving of minimum violations. [Sustained Dire]
No meat in the mountain passes. Gundabad's Orcs are eating bark and gristle and the look in their eyes has shifted from hungry to dangerous. Someone is going to regret this shortage.
The kill ran out two days ago. The mountain Orcs of Gundabad are surviving on spite and cold air, which is not as different from their normal diet as one might hope.

Empty racks in the Gundabad column. The warlords are looking at the prisoner escort with an assessment that goes beyond guard duty. Someone needs to resupply this column before the Orcs make their own arrangements.
The mountain scavengers strip their kill to bone and keep moving. Gundabad wastes nothing — not flesh, not time, not mercy.
Kill divided fast among the Gundabad ranks. Mountain Orcs do not linger over food — they consume it and move, the way they consume everything.
Meat from the last kill, still warm. The Orcs of Gundabad eat with the focused brutality of creatures raised inside a mountain where everything must be taken and nothing is given.

The racks are groaning under surplus kill. Gundabad's warlords distribute the excess without ceremony — in the mountains, food is power, and right now the column holds more power than it needs. [Rations: Surplus]

More meat than even Gundabad's appetite can clear in one march. The mountain Orcs eat until they cannot and then eat more. The warlords watch the surplus with the satisfaction of people who expect to run out of everything and haven't yet. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus kill from an exceptional hunt, divided through the Gundabad ranks with unusual generosity. When mountain Orcs have more than they need, they move faster — as though speed is the only way to spend excess. [Rations: Surplus]
Gundabad's cages are full to the crossbars. The mountain warlords feast on conquest and captive alike — and the rank and file smell victory in every chain that rattles. [Captive Spoils +5]
The cages overflow and the warlords are satisfied. Gundabad measures success in captives and plunder — and today both columns are full. [Captive Spoils +5]
Full cages, rattling chains, and the mountain warlords in good humour. For the Orcs of Gundabad, this is exactly what a successful campaign looks like. [Captive Spoils +5]
