Enough prisoners to make the march worthwhile, not so many they become a problem. Gundabad measures success in chain-links. [Prisoners in Column +2]
Captives in hand, march moving. The mountain Orcs accept the tally without enthusiasm and without complaint — which, for them, is practically contentment. [Prisoners in Column +2]
The prisoner count is acceptable. Gundabad's warlords note it, pocket the calculation, and keep marching.
Few prisoners walk behind. Gundabad's warlords grow restless — conquest without tribute is just a walk in the cold, and nobody marched from the mountains for that. [Prisoner Burden -5]
Empty chains behind the column. The mountain Orcs came down from Gundabad for spoils and have found very little. The warlords are running out of patience. [Prisoner Burden -5]
No captives. No tribute. The cold of the mountain is in every soldier's bones, and so is the knowledge that they have nothing to show for it. [Prisoner Burden -5]
Deep winter and the cages are full. Gundabad thrives in the cold dark — this is the mountain at its most itself, and its servants are grimly, brutally satisfied. [Faction Peak]
Winter in the mountains, meat plentiful, cages full. The Orcs of Gundabad are in their element — dark, cold, and entirely at home. [Faction Peak]
Gundabad's finest season: deep cold, full racks, full cages. The warlords count their wealth in chains and find it satisfactory. [Faction Peak]
Empty bellies and empty cages in the mountain cold. The Gundabad warlords are starting to question the expedition — when Orcs start questioning, something bleeds. [Faction Dire]
No meat, no prisoners, deep winter. The mountain Orcs are cold and hungry and have nothing to show for the march — a combination that rarely ends without violence. [Faction Dire]
Empty racks and empty chains in the worst cold of the season. Gundabad's warlords are meeting. Those meetings, historically, produce new leaders and fewer questions. [Faction Dire]

Spring thaws the mountain passes and the Gundabad war-bands come down from their winter fortresses. The raids begin in spring — always in spring — when the passes clear and the lowland settlements are not yet ready.

The Misty Mountains open in spring and Gundabad's appetite turns outward. The warlords begin planning the season's raids with the focused enthusiasm of creatures who have been cooped up in mountain tunnels for four months.
Ice breaks on the high passes and the Orcs of Gundabad emerge into the spring air. They are hungry, restless, and have had all winter to plan. The lowlands should be concerned.
High summer and the mountain passes stay open longest in this season. Gundabad's raids run deepest in summer — the Orcs range far when the weather permits, and the weather currently permits.

Midsummer warmth reaches even the high passes of the Misty Mountains. The Orcs of Gundabad use the long days to push further than usual, driven by the mountain instinct to take what the good season offers.
Summer in the mountains — the warmest it gets, which is still cold enough to be unpleasant for anyone who isn't a mountain Orc. The Gundabad column moves fast in the clement weather.

Autumn closes the high passes early in the Misty Mountains. Gundabad begins pulling back to the fortress — the raids wind down, the stores are counted, and the warlords plan the winter in the way all Gundabad planning happens: grimly and with full accounting of losses.
The mountain cold returns in autumn before it does in the lowlands. Gundabad's war-bands are moving back to the passes — one last push before the winter seals the roads.

Autumn in the Misty Mountains. Gundabad's soldiers know what's coming — they always do. They push the last of the autumn campaign with the specific energy of creatures who know the cold is only weeks away.
Deep winter in the Misty Mountains — cold enough to stop most armies and cold enough to feel like home to Gundabad. The Orcs are in their element and the fortress is full. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Snow on every peak and ice in every pass. Gundabad's fortress is sealed from the outside world and its soldiers operate with the focused brutality of creatures in their native environment. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

The mountain winter is Gundabad's season. The Orcs know these cold, dark passes better than anyone — they were built here, in the dark and the cold. Everything else is foreign territory. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Three days of Gundabad at its mountain-fortress best — full cages, full racks, deep cold. The warlords are grimly satisfied and the Orcs are as close to content as Gundabad's soldiers ever come. [Sustained Peak]

The mountain fortress and its soldiers have held peak for three days. Gundabad in three-day surplus is a fearsome thing — well-fed, warm enough, and looking outward for what to take next. [Sustained Peak]

Three consecutive days of the Misty Mountain's finest campaign conditions. The Orcs of Gundabad are operating exactly as the mountain made them — cold, relentless, and currently winning. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of empty cages and empty racks. Gundabad's warlords are very close to the conversation where someone challenges someone for leadership. The column has three more days before that conversation becomes inevitable. [Sustained Dire]

The third day running. The mountain Orcs are eating less and thinking more, which in Gundabad is the specific combination that precedes the kind of violence that solves problems by making different problems. [Sustained Dire]

Three days in and the situation is unchanged. Gundabad's patience is measured in meal cycles, not days, and the meal cycles have all come up short. Something is going to give — the only question is what. [Sustained Dire]

The shadow-fed hunts have failed. The servants of Dol Guldur go without, which in the darkness under Mirkwood means something beyond hunger — the Necromancer's displeasure is its own kind of starvation.
Empty racks beneath the fortress. The creatures of Dol Guldur have stopped moving at full pace and the dungeons seem darker for it — not metaphorically. The shadow thins when its servants are unfed.
Three days without kill. The hunters of Dol Guldur return empty-handed from the Mirkwood darkness and the Necromancer's patience is being spent faster than his provisions.
Fed on darkness and raw kill beneath the shadow of the old fortress. The hunters of Dol Guldur are sustained by the Necromancer's will as much as by flesh.
Kill from the Mirkwood hunt, divided in silence. The servants of the dark fortress eat without fire — light is not welcome here, and neither is warmth.
Meat from the shadow hunts, passed through the ranks beneath the rotting eaves. The creatures of Dol Guldur eat as they do everything — in darkness, without acknowledgement.

The Mirkwood hunts were exceptional and the shadow-larder is overflowing. The creatures of Dol Guldur eat beyond their need and become more than they were — the Necromancer's power feeds on surplus as much as on want. [Rations: Surplus]
More kill than the fortress can store in a week. The servants of the dark tower eat deep and the darkness deepens with them. A well-fed Dol Guldur is a more dangerous Dol Guldur. [Rations: Surplus]
Surplus from exceptional shadow-hunts. The Necromancer's servants are fed beyond expectation and the darkness around the old fortress is thicker and more present for it. [Rations: Surplus]
The dungeons of Dol Guldur grow crowded. The shadow feeds — and the servants of the Necromancer grow bolder when they know the dark lord's larder is full. [Captive Spoils +5]
Full dungeons beneath Mirkwood. The shadow deepens when the cages fill — and the servants of Dol Guldur grow stronger for it. [Captive Spoils +5]
The old fortress's cells are at capacity. Somewhere in the darkness, the Necromancer is pleased — and his pleasure is felt in the strength of every servant. [Captive Spoils +5]
A steady stream of captives flows into the dark halls beneath Mirkwood. The Necromancer's operations proceed — quietly, methodically, without mercy. [Prisoners in Column +2]
Captives moving to the dungeons at a sustainable rate. Dol Guldur's shadow does not rush — it accumulates. [Prisoners in Column +2]

The prisoner column feeds the fortress at its usual pace. The dark works of Dol Guldur proceed as they have always proceeded — steadily, silently, and without account to anyone. [Prisoners in Column +2]
The cages beneath Dol Guldur sit empty. The Necromancer is displeased — and when the shadow is displeased, its servants feel it in their bones like a blade in winter. [Prisoner Burden -5]
Empty cells and a displeased shadow. The darkness of Dol Guldur is thinner when unfed — and the servants feel that thinness as a kind of cold that doesn't leave. [Prisoner Burden -5]
Nothing for the dungeons. The Necromancer's hunger is not satisfied — and unsatisfied hunger, at this level of darkness, is everyone else's problem. [Prisoner Burden -5]

Autumn deepens over Mirkwood and the Dol Guldur dungeons overflow. The shadow is at its most potent. Raw flesh and fresh captives — the Necromancer's servants have never been more content with their work. [Faction Peak]
The old darkness is well-fed and the cages are full at exactly the right season. Dol Guldur's shadow stretches further under autumn — and this autumn it stretches far indeed. [Faction Peak]
Autumn mists, full dungeons, and meat in the ranks. The fortress under Mirkwood is operating exactly as designed, which is to say: terrifyingly well. [Faction Peak]

The meat is gone and the cages are bare. The shadow under Mirkwood is displeased — not loudly, not dramatically. Just that cold, deep sense that the Eye is watching, and the Eye has found wanting. [Faction Dire]
Empty cells and empty racks in the shadow of Dol Guldur. The darkness is thin tonight — and a thin darkness is an angry darkness. [Faction Dire]
Nothing for the fortress. The Necromancer's hunger goes unsatisfied and the servants feel the cold of his displeasure in ways that are difficult to describe and impossible to ignore. [Faction Dire]

Spring light reaches even the shadow of Dol Guldur, which the Necromancer's servants find deeply inconvenient. The darkness thins in spring and the old fortress pulls inward, waiting for the light to pass.
The spring stirs things in Mirkwood that the servants of the dark would prefer remained unstirred. The wood-elves range further in spring, and Dol Guldur is more watched. The shadow moves carefully.

Spring in Mirkwood and the old darkness retreats slightly from the brightest paths. The creatures of Dol Guldur work around the light as they always have — patiently, persistently, and without acknowledgement.

High summer and even Mirkwood's canopy admits more light than usual. The servants of Dol Guldur operate on reduced hours, avoiding the brightest parts of the day, and compensate by being more dangerous in the dark.

Midsummer above the old fortress. The darkness holds inside the ruin but the world outside is too light for comfort. The Necromancer's servants wait for autumn with the patience of things that have been waiting since the First Age.
Summer light reaches further into Mirkwood than is healthy for Dol Guldur's operations. The shadow adapts — always adapts — but the Necromancer's servants move with slightly more caution than usual.

Autumn comes to Mirkwood and the shadow of Dol Guldur reaches its furthest extent of the year. The creatures of the old fortress feel the season as a returning — darkness at its most powerful, the Necromancer at his most present. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

The great forest darkens in autumn and the old fortress deepens into its shadow. This is Dol Guldur's finest season — autumn shadow over a dying wood, the Necromancer's power at full stretch. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Autumn under Mirkwood and the darkness is thick and complete. The servants of the old fortress move most freely now — the shadow is at its fullest and the old terror at its most potent. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Winter closes the Mirkwood paths and the old fortress settles into cold silence. The darkness of Dol Guldur is most opaque in winter — the shadow does not thin in cold the way it does in warmth.
Snow on the rotten eaves of the old fortress and cold in the dungeons. The Necromancer's servants feel winter as a deepening rather than a hardship — cold suits what they serve.
Deep winter under Mirkwood. The dungeons are cold and the hunts are harder in snow — but the shadow is thick enough to compensate, and the creatures of Dol Guldur operate by its light.

Three days of autumn shadow at its absolute maximum — full dungeons, full larder, the Necromancer at his most present. Dol Guldur has been operating in peak darkness for three consecutive days, and the forest feels it. [Sustained Peak]

The old fortress has held its peak for three days. The shadow is deepest it has been since the Necromancer first settled here. The creatures below the rotten eaves move with a confidence that goes beyond well-fed. [Sustained Peak]
Three days of Dol Guldur at its most terrible — autumn dark, full cages, Necromancer's hunger satisfied. The great forest has not been this afraid in a long time. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of empty dungeons and empty larder under the failing shadow. The Necromancer's displeasure has lasted three full days, and in Dol Guldur, three days of divine disapproval is not symbolic — it is felt in the body. [Sustained Dire]

The third day of the old fortress's worst stretch. The shadow is thin and the servants are going without. The darkness under Mirkwood has not been this diminished since Gandalf first asked uncomfortable questions about it. [Sustained Dire]

Three days running and the shadow has not recovered. Dol Guldur endures — it always endures — but something fundamental in the Necromancer's operation has stopped working for three full days, and that has never ended quietly. [Sustained Dire]
The olive jars are empty and the corsairs are starting to comment on it, which in Umbarian terms means the grumbling has moved from personal to political.
Nothing in the hold provisions. The Corsairs of Umbar are accustomed to taking what they need — but there is nothing to take on this road, and the realization is sharpening tempers.
Three days without the good oil. The Umbarian sailors are eating dry and walking instead of sailing, and neither condition suits creatures built for raiding the comfortable. Something must change.
Olive jars cracked open from the corsair holds — plundered from southern ports and carried across the sea. The Umbarians eat well before the blood starts.
Corsair olives, pressed and pickled from the Bay of Belfalas groves. The sailors of Umbar eat with the satisfaction of men who took what they're eating from someone who didn't want to give it.
Salt olives from the southern holds, divided among the crew. Every jar is plunder and every bite is a reminder of why the Corsairs sail.

The holds are overloaded with olive jars — more than the campaign requires by half. The Corsairs eat with the generous excess of people who have recently raided somewhere that packed well. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus olive oil and pickled goods, stacked higher in the provision carts than is technically advisable. The Umbarian captains note the surfeit and calculate what it could have sold for. They eat it anyway. [Rations: Surplus]

Every hold full of Belfalas olives and the corsairs eating freely. Umbar at genuine surplus is a fleet in a good mood — which is still a dangerous fleet, but one that is temporarily interested in things other than violence. [Rations: Surplus]
The slave holds overflow and the corsair merchants are doing the mental arithmetic of profit. Every chain represents future gold, and the sailors fight harder for knowing it. [Captive Spoils +5]
Full holds and full ledgers. Umbar's merchants are counting their future profits with the focused joy of people who have just had a very good week of raiding. [Captive Spoils +5]
The slave count is excellent and the captains are already negotiating prices. Umbar's economy runs on this, and right now it is running very smoothly. [Captive Spoils +5]
A workable haul of prisoners in the holds. The corsairs are satisfied — not ecstatic, but the ledger looks reasonable and that is enough. [Prisoners in Column +2]
Captives in hand, holds reasonably full. The Umbarian captains note the tally and find it acceptable — not worth celebrating, but not worth complaining about either. [Prisoners in Column +2]
The prisoner count meets quota. Umbar operates on quotas and margins — and currently, both are within range. [Prisoners in Column +2]

The slave holds lie nearly empty and the Umbarian merchants are growing impatient. Corsairs do not sail for the glory of it — bring them stock, or expect the grumbling to get much louder. [Prisoner Burden -5]
Empty holds and unhappy merchants. The Corsairs of Umbar run their operation on prisoner intake, and intake has stopped. The numbers don't work and the sailors know it. [Prisoner Burden -5]

Nothing in the holds. The ledgers are red, the captains are terse, and the crew is beginning to wonder if this voyage is profitable. It is not a good question for a corsair captain to hear. [Prisoner Burden -5]
High summer over the Bay of Belfalas, the olive harvest is exceptional, and the holds are full of cargo that will make Umbar rich this season. The corsairs are almost cheerful. Almost. [Faction Peak]
Summer, full olive jars, full slave holds. The Corsairs of Umbar are at the height of their operational efficiency — and everyone on this fleet can smell the profit from here. [Faction Peak]

The Bay is calm, the olives are exceptional, and the holds are full. Umbar has not had a season this profitable since the last time someone wasn't paying attention to their harbour defences. [Faction Peak]

The olive jars are empty and so are the holds. Corsairs with nothing to sell and nothing to eat start making their own arrangements — and nobody in this fleet wants to find out what those arrangements are. [Faction Dire]
Empty jars, empty holds, unhappy crew. A corsair fleet in this state is one bad day from a mutiny — and the days have not been good lately. [Faction Dire]
No olives, no prisoners, no profit. The Corsairs of Umbar did not leave port for a voyage that breaks even. Right now they are not breaking even. They are breaking other things. [Faction Dire]
Spring winds on the Bay of Belfalas and the corsair fleet is ready to sail. The trading — and raiding — season opens in spring, and the Corsairs of Umbar treat both with equal professional attention.
The spring seas open the shipping lanes and the Umbarian captains are studying the charts. Every vessel that moves in spring can be assessed for value. The corsairs are always assessing.
Spring on the bay — the weather turns and the opportunity opens. Umbar's sailors feel the season as a beginning: new routes, new targets, new ledger entries that haven't been made yet.

High summer over the Bay of Belfalas — long days, warm seas, and the olive harvest approaching peak. The Corsairs of Umbar are making money and spending it on preparation for making more money. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Midsummer and the Belfalas olives are at their finest. The corsair fleet is at maximum operational range in summer, the seas are clear, and the pickings are abundant. This is Umbar's finest season. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Summer heat on the southern sea and the olive groves heavy with fruit. The Corsairs of Umbar in high summer are at their most profitable and most dangerous. The bay knows to be careful. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Autumn brings the last of the season's good sailing weather. The Corsairs make one more major run before winter closes the shipping lanes — the autumn raid is always the most ambitious one.
The season turns and the Bay of Belfalas grows rougher. Umbarian captains have been sailing these waters for generations and they read the autumn swells like text — time to make final arrangements.
Autumn on the bay — the Corsairs are preparing for the long winter port season. The final trades are made, the final raids assessed, and the holds are counted before the cold counts them for you.

Winter in Umbar — the port city's busiest season. The corsairs are in harbour, the deals are being made, and the olive oil trade is running through every tavern in the lower city. A different kind of campaign.
Winter closes the long-range routes but the bay remains active. Umbarian merchants run their winter books while the corsair captains plan the spring raids. The city never fully stops.
Cold winter in the southern port. The Corsairs of Umbar are in their element even in winter — Umbar trades in every season, and trading is what they are. The hold goods are moving.

Three days of Umbar at its most prosperous — full holds, summer seas, and olives at peak. The corsair fleet is operating at the maximum intersection of supply and opportunity. The captains are not modest about this. [Sustained Peak]

The Corsairs have sustained peak performance for three days. Summer surplus and full slave holds — the Umbarian ledgers have not looked this good since the last really successful raid on the northern coast. [Sustained Peak]

Three days running at the top of Umbar's considerable capability. The corsair captains are not celebrating — that would invite questions — but the numbers tell the story, and the story is exceptional. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of empty holds and empty jars. The corsair captains are becoming creative in their assessment of what the column could be doing instead of this. None of their ideas are reassuring. [Sustained Dire]

The third consecutive day of negative margin. Umbarian sailors operate on the principle that the sea always provides — but the sea has not provided, and the alternative provides for the sea instead. [Sustained Dire]
Three days and the fleet is not recovering. The Corsairs of Umbar have a word for an expedition that costs more than it earns: over. They are beginning to use it. [Sustained Dire]
The fruit packs are empty. The Haradrim war-chiefs don't announce it — they simply march harder, as though pace is a substitute for provision. In the deep south, it sometimes is.
Three days without the sweet fruit of the palm groves. The desert warriors are running on heat and pride, both of which are available in abundance. Neither is quite as sustaining as the fruit was.

The provision sacks have nothing left from Harad's groves. The southern warriors are eating what the road offers — which is very little — and pushing forward on the old southern fuel: the desire to prove they can.
Sweetness of the deep south — dried fruit of Harad's palm groves, carried through the desert heat. The war-chiefs eat as conquerors.
Southern fruit dried in Harad's sun and packed in woven sacks. The soldiers of the war-chiefs eat what their homeland grows — hot, sweet, and touched by the Oliphaunt trails.
Haradrim fruit passed through the ranks in the morning heat. The desert warriors eat without complaint — in the south, you eat what the land gives you, and you are grateful for the fire in it.

The fruit sacks overflow — Harad's finest harvest packed without restraint. The southern war-chiefs eat twice over and still the sacks are heavy. This is what desert abundance looks like when the season is right. [Rations: Surplus]
Surplus from the palm groves, packed beyond the column's need. The Haradrim eat with the focused gratitude of people who know exactly what drought looks like, and this is not it. [Rations: Surplus]

The provision train is overloaded with Haradrim fruit — sweet, heavy, and more than enough. The desert warriors eat in the morning heat with something approaching joy. A southern army in surplus is a very confident army. [Rations: Surplus]
The war-chief's pens are full. Harad grows rich on captive labour and proud on the sight of the defeated. The warriors march with the swagger of conquerors. [Captive Spoils +5]
Full pens, satisfied war-chiefs, and warriors who know the campaign is delivering. Harad measures a leader by what he brings back — and what is coming back is considerable. [Captive Spoils +5]

The captive count exceeds expectations and the war-chiefs are counting their future worth. Southern prosperity is measured in what you have taken, and today the measure is generous. [Captive Spoils +5]
The column carries a respectable number of prisoners. Harad's war-chiefs note it with satisfaction — not victory, but a promising instalment toward it. [Prisoners in Column +2]
Captives in hand, column moving south. The Haradrim manage their prisoners with the efficient cruelty of a people who have been taking slaves since before Gondor stood. [Prisoners in Column +2]
The prisoner tally meets the war-chief's minimum. Harad does not celebrate adequate results — it catalogues them and moves on to the next campaign. [Prisoners in Column +2]
The war-chief demands captives and the pens stand idle. Harad does not respect an army that returns empty-handed — and the warriors know it. [Prisoner Burden -5]
Empty pens and a war-chief who is counting nothing. In the south, an army that takes nothing is an army that proves nothing — and proving nothing is nearly as bad as losing. [Prisoner Burden -5]

No captives for the southern pens. The Haradrim warriors are marching back with their pride intact and nothing else — and in Harad, pride alone does not justify the campaign cost. [Prisoner Burden -5]
High summer in Harad, and the fruit is at its sweetest. The pens are full and the war-chiefs are satisfied. This is the south as it was meant to be: hot, abundant, and victorious. [Faction Peak]

Summer heat, full fruit sacks, full pens. The Haradrim are operating at the height of their campaigning season and they know it. War-chiefs do not often smile — but they are smiling now. [Faction Peak]

The desert is at its most generous and the campaign at its most successful. Harad's warriors eat fruit in the sun and count their captives with the satisfaction of men who have earned both. [Faction Peak]

The fruit is spent and the pens are empty in the desert heat. The southern warriors grow restless without plunder or provision — and in Harad, restless warriors are a political problem. [Faction Dire]
Empty fruit sacks and empty pens. The heat of Harad is merciless — and so are the war-chiefs when a campaign fails to produce. Both are currently in evidence. [Faction Dire]
No fruit, no captives, and a desert that doesn't care. The Haradrim warriors have marched this far for nothing they can show a war-chief — and that conversation is coming. [Faction Dire]

Spring in the desert is brief and beautiful. The Haradrim call it the time of the brief flower — the desert blooms for a fortnight, then returns to its proper severity. The war-chiefs move during the bloom.
The desert spring comes and goes like a rumour. The Haradrim use the mild weeks for the furthest-ranging parts of the campaign — it's the only season the deep desert is passable without cost.

Brief spring over Harad. The war-bands move in the mild weather with an efficiency that the harsh seasons make impossible. The pale flowers last three weeks. The campaigns they enable last much longer.

High summer in Harad and the sun is absolute. The Haradrim are built for exactly this — the heat is a condition of their nature, not a hardship, and the fruit is at its peak sweetness. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Midsummer in the deep south. The palm groves are heavy with fruit and the war-chiefs are at full strength. Summer is when Harad campaigns and Harad campaigning is something the northern lands have learned to take seriously. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
The southern sun at its most merciless and the Haradrim at their best. Summer fruit, summer heat, summer warriors — the desert at full power moving toward its objectives. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Autumn in Harad — the heat eases fractionally and the war-chiefs count their season's gains. The autumn accounting is important in the south: it sets the tribute numbers, the raid tallies, the debt balances.

The season turns in the deep south and the Haradrim begin to think about what comes next. Autumn is for consolidation — take what the summer gave, protect it against the winter, and plan for a better summer.
Autumn caravans moving through Harad. The desert is slightly less hostile in autumn, and slightly less hostile is all the Haradrim need to extend their operations further than the summer allowed.

Winter in the deep south is something northern peoples would call a pleasant autumn. The Haradrim, for whom it is the coldest season, pull on their heavier robes and prepare for the three coldest months they know.

Winter reaches even the deep south, in its thin way. The Haradrim acknowledge the cold by adding a layer and reducing the pace fractionally. The war-chiefs keep to their plans — the mild winter of the south barely warrants adjustment.

Cold season in Harad — not cold by any standard except the Haradrim's own. The southern warriors march in winter without complaint, because in the south, this is not actually winter. It is just a slightly less hot autumn.

Three days of the south at its absolute finest — summer surplus, full pens, the desert at peak. The Haradrim war-chiefs are calculating their tribute with the satisfaction of people who have not been disappointed in three consecutive days. [Sustained Peak]

The southern campaign has maintained peak for three days. Fruit, captives, summer heat — Harad operating at its designed capacity. The war-chiefs are beginning to let themselves believe the season is exceptional. [Sustained Peak]

Three days running of Harad at its best. The desert warriors are well-fed and well-rewarded. In the south, this kind of sustained success creates the kind of leader-legends that last for generations. [Sustained Peak]

Three days without provision and without tribute. The desert is unforgiving of weakness, and the Haradrim war-chiefs know the column looks weak right now. Three more days of this and the look will be correct. [Sustained Dire]

The third consecutive day of shortfall. In the deep south, sustained failure has a specific political consequence: the war-chief stops being war-chief. The current one is aware of this arithmetic. [Sustained Dire]

Three days and nothing has improved. The Haradrim endure because the desert teaches endurance above everything else — but endurance has a cost, and three days of this has been paying it. [Sustained Dire]
The cheese is gone. The Variags of Khand have run the numbers and found the margin unacceptable. A mercenary column without provisions is a breach of the operational contract, and breaches are noted.
Three days without the clay-vessel rations. The Variags are professionals — they are continuing to march, because that is what they are being paid to do — but the invoice is being mentally revised.
Empty saddlebags and an empty ledger where the provision line should be. The Variags of Khand are running a campaign that is currently costing more than it is generating. This is not sustainable.
Hard cheese from the plateau of Khand, aged in clay vessels and carried on the saddle-horn. The Variags are mercenaries — they waste nothing and complain about nothing.
Khand cheese divided among the riders. It keeps long and travels well — exactly the qualities the Variags value in everything they carry, including their loyalty.

Clay-sealed cheese from the high plateau, cracked open at the midday halt. The Variags eat with the methodical efficiency of soldiers who have learned that food is a cost of operations, not a pleasure.

The provision panniers are overloaded with Khand cheese — more than the march requires. The Variags eat more than the standard ration and note the surplus as a contractual positive. The march is performing above projection. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus clay-vessel cheese from an unusually well-supplied depot. The Variags of Khand eat their fill and calculate the per-day savings against the contract rate. The numbers are good. The march is good. [Rations: Surplus]

More cheese than the column can consume in a fortnight, packed by a quartermaster who understood Variag operational requirements. The mercenaries are eating well and moving better. This is what the contract was supposed to look like. [Rations: Surplus]
Khand counts its captives as currency — and the ledger looks good. The Variags respect results, and right now the results are marching in chains behind them. [Captive Spoils +5]
The prisoner count is excellent by mercenary standards. The Variags of Khand are calculating their fees against the haul and finding the margin favourable. [Captive Spoils +5]
Full chains and a satisfied client. The Variags operate on deliverables, and the deliverables have been delivered — in quantity. [Captive Spoils +5]
A reasonable haul of prisoners for a mercenary operation of this size. The Variags calculate their day's work and find it acceptable.
Captives moving at a pace the Variags consider professionally adequate. Not exceptional. Not embarrassing. Professionally adequate. [Prisoners in Column +2]
The prisoner tally is within the contracted range. The Variags of Khand do not celebrate adequate performance — they invoice for it. [Prisoners in Column +2]
Empty chains are worthless chains. The Variags ride for profit, and right now the profit column is blank. A mercenary without spoils starts to wonder who's paying and why. [Prisoner Burden -5]
No prisoners, no profit, no reason to continue at the agreed rate. The Variags of Khand are already composing the renegotiation in their heads. [Prisoner Burden -5]

Empty chains and a client who is not getting what they paid for. The Variags are professionals — and professionals track their failures the same way they track their successes. This one is tracked. [Prisoner Burden -5]

Autumn curing season and the cheese is in full supply. The prisoner count is excellent by mercenary standards. The Variags of Khand are about as happy as people who treat happiness as a business calculation can be. [Faction Peak]
Khand cheese and a very good prisoner tally in the harvest season. The Variags are running the numbers and the numbers are running in their favour. A rare and treasured condition. [Faction Peak]

Autumn, full cheese stores, maximum prisoner intake. The Variags of Khand are operating at professional peak. They would not call it joy — but the invoices will reflect something very close to it. [Faction Peak]
The cheese is nearly gone and so is the profit margin. Empty cages and empty stomachs make for contract renegotiations — and the Variags' rates are about to go up considerably. [Faction Dire]

No cheese, no captives, negative margin. The Variags of Khand are professionals, and a professional knows when to renegotiate, when to walk, and when both options are unavailable. They are currently assessing. [Faction Dire]
Empty stores, empty chains, unhappy accountants. The Variags measure everything — and right now, everything measures poorly. [Faction Dire]

Spring thaws the high plateau of Khand and the mercenary contracts begin arriving. The Variags come down from their winter positions with their rates already set for the season. Spring is when the hiring happens.

The plateau opens in spring and the Variags begin moving toward whoever is paying. This season's contracts have been reviewed — the terms are acceptable, the advance has been paid, and the column is moving.

Spring on the roads from Khand. The Variags are professional about seasons the way they are professional about everything — spring means contract season, and contract season means the column is deployed.
Midsummer and the mercenary trade is at its peak. The Variags are in demand in summer — every faction's campaign season needs professional soldiers, and the Variags supply what demand requires.
High summer and the operational tempo is at maximum. The Variags of Khand are meeting their contractual deliverables at the height of campaign season. The cheese is good and so are the margins.

Summer heat and full operational pace. The Variags are earning their rate in summer — the hardest season for campaigning, the most lucrative, and the one where professional soldiers prove their value most clearly.

Autumn on the plateau roads and the Khand cheese is in peak curing season. The Variags are provisioned at their best and winding down the summer contracts toward winter arrangements. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
The curing season in Khand — when the cheese is at its finest and the autumn contracts come due. The Variags eat well in autumn and settle their seasonal accounts. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Autumn provisioning from the high plateau. The Khand cheese reaches peak quality and the Variag column is running at its best operational margin of the year. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Winter on the high plateau of Khand and the contract work dries up. The Variags spend winter in maintenance: equipment, training, contract review. Not every season can be lucrative. They plan for that.
Cold season on the plateau roads. The Variags are between significant contracts in winter and they use the downtime the way professionals use downtime — preparing for the next deployment.
Winter in Khand. The Variags hold their positions, review their contracts, and eat cheese. They have always been practical about winter — it is simply the season when the margins are thinner.

Three days at peak operational performance. The Variags of Khand have sustained exceptional margin for three consecutive days — full cheese, maximum captive intake, autumn curing season. The invoice for this campaign is going to look very good. [Sustained Peak]

The Variags have held their peak for three days. Khand cheese and captive surplus sustained across three separate daily accountings. This is the kind of streak that gets cited in future contract negotiations. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of Variag excellence. The plateau mercenaries are operating at a standard that justifies their rate and then some. Whatever is being paid for this campaign is being earned at a factor the client should appreciate. [Sustained Peak]

Three consecutive days of negative margin. The Variags of Khand are professionals, and professionals do not operate at a loss indefinitely. Three days is almost exactly the threshold at which renegotiation becomes inevitable. [Sustained Dire]

The third day of underperformance. The Variags have been evaluating their contractual obligations against current deliverables for three days now, and the evaluation is increasingly unfavourable to continued compliance. [Sustained Dire]

Three days of costs exceeding returns. The Variag ledger is in deficit and the mercenaries know it. The window for corrections is closing. After this window closes, the Variags will make different kinds of corrections. [Sustained Dire]
The salt-meat ran out three days ago. The Easterlings are marching on wind and east-plain stubbornness, which sustains further than outsiders expect but cannot sustain indefinitely.

Empty saddlebags on the eastern march. The Dragon-helm warriors are used to campaigning lean — but the eastern lords measure their tribute-collectors' results, and a hungry army produces thin results.

No salt-meat and the Rhûn tribute schedule waits for no army's supply problems. The Easterlings push forward on the old eastern discipline — you deliver or you explain why not, and the second option costs more than the first.
Salted plainsmeat, torn and passed among the Dragon-helm warriors without fire or fanfare. On the eastern wind rides the old promise: conquest, tribute, and iron.
Eastern salt-meat divided on the march. The warriors of Rhûn eat as they fight — without ceremony, without waste, and ready to resume at a moment's notice.
Plainsmeat from the eastern steppes, cured and carried. The Dragon-helm's soldiers were raised on this — and on the understanding that eating well means campaigning well.

The salt-meat provisions are exceptional — more than the eastern march requires by a significant margin. The Easterlings eat full portions and still the panniers are heavy. The Dragon-helm's quartermaster overdelivered. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus cured meat from the eastern steppes, more than the tribute schedule requires and more than the column can clear in a week. The Easterlings eat well and march faster — east-plain abundance suits east-plain soldiers. [Rations: Surplus]

The provision carts are overloaded with Rhûn salt-meat and the Dragon-helm warriors are eating beyond their usual careful rations. A well-fed eastern army moves at a different pace. The eastern lords should note this. [Rations: Surplus]
Prisoners march east in chains. Rhun expands its tribute lists — and the Dragon-helm warriors know their lord will be pleased. No finer proof of conquest than a full cage. [Captive Spoils +5]
The tribute column is full and heading east. The Easterling lords will be satisfied — and a satisfied lord means a rewarded general. The warriors know this calculus. [Captive Spoils +5]
Full chains heading to Rhun. The eastern lords measure their vassals by what they send home — and right now, what is being sent home is considerable. [Captive Spoils +5]
A steady flow of captives heads east toward Rhun. The Easterlings are meeting their quotas — quietly efficient, as the Dragon-helm demands. [Prisoners in Column +2]
Captives moving east at quota pace. The Dragon-helm's warriors neither celebrate adequate tribute nor complain about it — they deliver it. [Prisoners in Column +2]
The eastern tribute column is at acceptable levels. The Easterling lords will note it in their records — and the records will not complain. [Prisoners in Column +2]
No chains drag behind the column. The eastern lords expect tribute in flesh and iron — and they are not receiving it. The Dragon-helm warriors grow sullen on the march. [Prisoner Burden -5]
Empty tribute column. The Easterling lords do not accept empty-handed returns gracefully. The Dragon-helm warriors are already preparing their explanations. [Prisoner Burden -5]
Nothing for Rhun. The eastern lords keep careful records of what arrives and what does not — and what does not arrive carries consequences that travel faster than the column. [Prisoner Burden -5]

Campaign season in the east — the plainsmeat is salted and plentiful, and the prisoner column stretches back to the horizon. The Dragon-helm warriors are doing exactly what they were bred to do. [Faction Peak]
Autumn on the eastern plains: full salt-meat, full tribute column. The Easterlings are campaigning at maximum effectiveness — the Dragon-helm has never been brighter. [Faction Peak]
Plentiful eastern meat and a tribute column the lords of Rhun will actually be pleased to receive. The Dragon-helm warriors are at the peak of their season and they know it. [Faction Peak]
The meat is gone and the eastern tribute is missing. The Easterlings march in autumn without supply or spoils — and the Dragon-helm lords are not known for their patience with failure. [Faction Dire]
Empty salt packs and empty tribute chains. The Easterlings have produced nothing for Rhun and nothing for the mess — both problems are being noticed. [Faction Dire]
No meat, no tribute, no good news heading east. The Dragon-helm warriors are rehearsing their explanations. The eastern lords are not known to enjoy explanations. [Faction Dire]

Spring thaws the eastern plains and the Easterlings begin their campaign season. The long roads to the west open in spring, and the Dragon-helm's armies move along them with the purposeful efficiency of people running a long-standing obligation.
The steppes green up in spring and the Easterling war-bands ride out. Spring is for reconnaissance — the summer campaigns are better planned when the spring riders have been further west and back.

Spring on the eastern plains. The Easterlings ride with the quiet confidence of a people who know these roads better than their enemies do. The Dragon-helm turns east to west for the first time since autumn.

High summer on the eastern plains — long marching days and the salt-meat lasting exactly as long as it was cured to last. The Easterlings are operating at full campaign pace. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Midsummer and the Dragon-helm's armies are at maximum range. The eastern plains are good for long, fast marches in summer, and the Easterlings use every hour of the long days. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

The summer campaign is at its height. The Easterlings are covering the distances the Dragon-helm's lords expect, with the provisions they brought, at the speed the tribute schedule requires. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Autumn in the east and the tribute columns turn for home. The Dragon-helm warriors know the autumn calculation: what was taken, what was spent, what must be reported. The math of eastern campaigns.
The campaign season winds down as autumn closes the plains. The Easterlings push one last time before the cold comes — the autumn tribute is the season's accounting, and the accounts must balance.

Cold approaching from the north and the last of the autumn campaigning. The Dragon-helm's warriors are moving fast — they know the eastern winter comes hard and early, and they want to be home when it does.
Winter on the eastern plains — the cold comes down from the far north and the Easterling camps hunker close. The Dragon-helm's soldiers know this winter, have always known it. They were built for it.

The deepest winter in the east. The plains are empty and the roads are frozen. The Easterlings are in winter quarters, maintaining, training, and counting the tribute they took in the autumn. Not a bad count.

Eastern winter. The steppes are white and silent and the Easterlings are content in their own cold way. This is the season for accounting and planning — the summer campaigns begin in the calculations made now.

Three days of the Dragon-helm at full operational capacity. Salt-meat, tribute, summer march — the eastern campaign is running exactly as Rhûn's lords require it to run, and has been running that way for three days. [Sustained Peak]

The Easterlings have sustained their peak for three days. The eastern tribute schedule is being met, the provisions are holding, and the Dragon-helm warriors are at the height of their considerable ability. [Sustained Peak]

Three days running of east-plain excellence. The Dragon-helm's armies are delivering exactly what the lords of Rhûn demand — and have been delivering it three days straight. This is what the eastern campaign is supposed to look like. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of eastern shortfall. The Dragon-helm's armies are still marching — they will always march — but the tribute numbers are wrong and have been wrong for three days, and the eastern lords keep records. [Sustained Dire]

The third day. The Easterlings push forward with east-plain stubbornness, which is not the same as east-plain optimism. The difference is important. The tribute is still coming up short. [Sustained Dire]

Three consecutive days of insufficient delivery. The Easterlings have been in this position before and survived it. The Dragon-helm's lords have been in this position before too, and they remember which generals did and did not correct it. [Sustained Dire]
The grain is running low. Rohirric soldiers on half-rations ride half as fast, and speed is everything to the Mark. The horses know first — they are always first to know when something is wrong.
Empty grain sacks on the Riddermark march. The Riders of Rohan are still riding — they will always ride — but the easy speed of a well-fed column has become the grinding pace of one making do.

Three days since the last full provision. The Rohirrim push through it as they push through everything: by riding harder. But there is a limit to what hard riding can substitute for, and grain is close to that limit.
The golden grain of the Eastfold, ground fresh before the march. Where the Riddermark rides, it rides well-fed — and the Riders do not slow for anything.
Rohan's grain, milled at dawn and baked by the time the sun clears the Wold. The Riders eat standing and mount up still chewing — this is the Riddermark.
Westfold wheat bread, coarse and filling, handed up to the saddle. The Men of the Mark eat as their fathers ate — on the move, before the horn sounds again.

The provision train carries enough Eastfold grain for twice the march. The Rohirrim eat well and the horses are fed on the surplus — a well-fed horse runs differently, and the column runs differently for it. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus from the golden Eastfold harvest — more grain than the Riders need, which means the Riders are eating beyond their usual measured rations. The column moves with the ease of an army that has genuinely enough. [Rations: Surplus]

Grain overflowing the provision carts and the Riders eating freely. The Riddermark in surplus is one of the few things that makes Rohirric soldiers slow down — to eat properly, before riding faster. [Rations: Surplus]
The column is burdened with captives that the Riders of the Mark were not made to manage. Eomer would say: let them go or deal with them cleanly. [Prisoner Burden -3]
Too many prisoners for cavalry that was not bred to guard anything on foot. The horses are restless and the Riders are distracted. Neither is the Riddermark at its best. [Prisoner Burden -3]
Chains dragging behind the Rohirrim column. The horses notice. So do the riders. Neither is designed for this, and it is beginning to show. [Prisoner Burden -3]
A handful of prisoners are kept at pace behind the column. The Rohirrim watch them without sentiment — honour, but not softness.
Captives are moving with the column. The Riders manage it in the way they manage all things that are beneath them: competently, and without enjoying it.
The prisoner escort is in hand. Rohan does not linger on what is already managed — the road ahead is more important than the chains behind.
The Riders of the Mark move swift and unchained. No burden drags the column — only the thunder of hooves and the green smell of the Riddermark. [Captive Spoils +3]
No prisoners slow the Rohirrim. The column gallops as it should gallop — free, fast, and with nothing behind it but its own dust. [Captive Spoils +3]
Clean hands and open country. The Mark rides unburdened today, and every horse feels it in the length of its stride. [Captive Spoils +3]
High summer in the Riddermark, the grain sacks full and the column riding free. The horn of Helm Hammerhand echoes somewhere in the men's hearts — and it sounds like victory. [Faction Peak]
Midsummer in the Riddermark: grain in every saddlebag, no chains in the column, and the plains stretching green to the horizon. The Rohirrim were made for days like this. [Faction Peak]
The Mark at its finest — summer, grain, and an unburdened gallop. Theoden King's host could not have asked for better marching conditions. [Faction Peak]
The grain is nearly spent and too many captives slow the march. The Mark does not suffer this well — Rohirrim who cannot ride fast are Rohirrim who are losing. [Faction Dire]
Half-rations and chained prisoners slowing the cavalry column. The Riddermark was not built for either. The horses know it and so do the men. [Faction Dire]
Empty grain bags and chains on the road. This is not how Rohan campaigns. This is not how Rohan does anything. And yet here it is. [Faction Dire]
Spring on the Riddermark and the foaling season begins. The Rohirrim count their new horses and the numbers are good. A cavalry nation measures its spring by horseflesh, not weather.
The Wold greens and the roads open. Spring in Rohan is about movement — everything that was frozen or contained through winter begins to move, and the Riders move with it.
Spring rides the Riddermark harder than any season. The plains open, the horses are fresh, and the Rohirrim are as restless after winter as their animals. The horn sounds cleaner in spring air.

High summer on the Riddermark — the grain stands gold and the Riders are at full campaign pace. This is what the Mark was built for: long light, fast horses, and grain in the saddlebag. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Midsummer and the Eastfold harvest is coming in. The Rohirrim campaign in summer with one ear always angled toward the fields — a good harvest means a well-provisioned winter. Good summer, good winter. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

The summer grain is almost ready and the Riders know it. Full provisions, warm nights, fast roads — the Riddermark at its campaign peak is a force that moves like the open plain itself. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Harvest time in the Eastfold and the Rohirrim are thinking of home. Autumn is the season of return — the summer campaigns wind down, the grain comes in, and the Riders who can, ride back to the Mark.

The Westfold stores are being packed for winter. Even on campaign the Riders of the Mark feel the pull of autumn — something in Rohirric blood knows when the harvesting should happen, and it wants to be there.

Autumn on the Riddermark. The great plains turn gold and amber, and the Rohirrim feel the season as both a beauty and a reminder that the good fighting weather is ending. They use every remaining day.
Winter on the plains — the wind from the Misty Mountains crosses without mercy. The Rohirrim endure it the way they endure everything: on horseback, moving, close together, and without complaint.

Snow on the Wold and ice on the Entwash fords. The Riders of the Mark cannot fly south like the geese — they winter in Edoras, or they winter in the field, and both require the same Rohirric stubbornness.

The long winter ride. The Rohirrim pull their thick riding cloaks close and keep the formation tight. The horses hate the cold and the riders hate to see the horses hate anything. They move fast to stay warm.

Three days of the Riddermark at full gallop — summer grain, clean march, Riders at their best. Something about this stretch feels like the old days before the shadow touched the Mark. [Sustained Peak]

The Rohirrim have held their peak for three days. Full grain, no chains, and the easy speed of an army that has exactly what it needs. Théoden's horse would have run for three days in conditions like these. [Sustained Peak]

Three consecutive days of Rohan marching as Rohan should march. The Riders and the Mark and the open plains working together as they were always meant to. This is what they fight for. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of this. The Riders of the Mark have never been built for slow marches and heavy burdens, and three days of both has left the column moving like something it was not meant to be. [Sustained Dire]

The third day of the worst of the Riddermark's campaign. The Rohirrim endure — they were built to endure — but the horses are restless and the men are quieter than they should be. Something must change. [Sustained Dire]

Three consecutive days of the Mark marching wrong. The Rohirrim do not complain — they are not made for complaint — but three days of empty saddlebags and heavy chains has done something to the column's stride that a single good day cannot fix. [Sustained Dire]

The smoke-barrels are empty. The Bardings of Dale are walking in the direction of where the fish should be and finding none. The practical mind adjusts to shortfall the way it adjusts to everything: by noting it, calculating the impact, and moving on.

Nothing in the provision carts from the Long Lake. Dale's soldiers are on short rations and they manage it with the same ledger-efficiency they bring to everything — but the ledger shows a deficit that needs addressing.

Three days without the smoked fish. The Bardings of Dale are still marching — they have always marched through difficult supply situations — but the empty barrel has been noted, the adjustment has been calculated, and someone is going to answer for it.
Long Lake trout, smoked over applewood and packed in salt. The Bardings of Dale have traded and fished these waters for generations — old skill, honest food, steady hands.
Esgaroth smoke-fish, wrapped tight and kept cool in the provision cart. King Brand's men eat the same as the fishermen of the Long Lake — and there is no shame in that.
Dale fish, packed before the march, distributed at midday. The taste of the Long Lake travels well, and the Bardings are grateful that it does.

The provision carts carry double the expected fish — a record Long Lake run, packed before departure. The Bardings of Dale are eating beyond their rations and the column is moving with the ease of an over-provisioned army. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus from Esgaroth's finest fishing season in a decade. The smoke-barrels are stacked three high and the Bardings eat generously. Dale was rebuilt to prosper — and right now, it is prospering. [Rations: Surplus]

More Long Lake fish than the march can consume in a fortnight. The Bardings distribute freely with the matter-of-fact generosity of people who understand supply chains and know that this one is, for once, exceptionally favourable. [Rations: Surplus]
More captives than the column can comfortably manage. Dale is a city of merchants and fair dealing — this many prisoners sits uneasily with Barding sensibilities. [Prisoner Burden -3]

The prisoner column has grown past Dale's capacity for managing it gracefully. The Bardings are practical people — and practically speaking, this is a problem with no clean solution. [Prisoner Burden -3]
Too many captives for the column's good conscience. Dale was rebuilt on trade and honest dealing — neither describes what is happening at the rear of this march. [Prisoner Burden -3]
A modest number of prisoners walk in the column's wake. The people of Dale process them with the same orderly practicality they bring to their market stalls.
Captives in hand, march moving. The Bardings approach the prisoner column with the same ledger-minded efficiency they apply to trade disputes — methodically and without emotion.
The prisoner escort is manageable. Dale has always found a way to keep things running — even things it would prefer not to be running.
The Bardings march with clean conscience and clear roads. No excess weight slows the column — only the long road to whatever comes next. [Captive Spoils +3]
No prisoners slow Dale's column today. The Bardings march as their city was rebuilt — forward, purposeful, and without unnecessary weight. [Captive Spoils +3]
Clean march from Dale. No chains, no burden, no delay. King Brand's soldiers move as the city of Dale trades — efficiently, and always with an eye on what's ahead. [Captive Spoils +3]
Autumn by the Long Lake: the fish are running, the salt stores are full, and the column marches free. King Brand would approve of a march this well-provisioned. [Faction Peak]

The smoke-barrels are full and the column moves without chains in the best fishing season of the year. The Bardings of Dale have known worse — and are glad, in their practical way, that this is not one of those times. [Faction Peak]
Autumn harvest and unburdened soldiers. Dale at its finest — provisioned by the Long Lake and unencumbered by the worst of what war leaves behind. [Faction Peak]
The smoked fish is gone and the captive count is too high. Dale has survived worse — Smaug, for instance — but this particular combination of problems is making the march unpleasant. [Faction Dire]
Empty fish barrels and too many prisoners. The Bardings of Dale know how to rebuild from devastation — but they would prefer not to have to, especially not twice in the same season. [Faction Dire]
No smoke-fish and a column slowed by captives. Dale's practical sensibilities are being tested in ways that no market ledger was ever designed to account for. [Faction Dire]

The Long Lake thaws in spring and the fish begin to run. Dale's season opens with the thaw — the nets go out, the smoke-houses fire, and the city comes alive in the specific way of a trading city waking from winter. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Spring on the Long Lake and the first boats are out. The Bardings feel the season as a business beginning — new routes, new stock, new ledger entries. Spring is when Dale makes its year. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

The ice breaks on Esgaroth's piers and the fish are running. Spring provisions are the best of the year and the Bardings of Dale march with the energy of people who know their supply chain has just opened back up. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

High summer on the Long Lake — the trading season is at its height and the Bardings are moving goods in both directions at once. Even soldiers from Dale think in terms of trade routes. They can't help it.

Midsummer and the lake is alive with boats and business. The Bardings of Dale operate with the bustling efficiency of their home city — purposeful, rapid, and never more than one conversation away from a transaction.
Long summer days on the roads from Dale. The Bardings use every hour of the long light for travel and trade — summer is when distance costs least and time rewards most.

Autumn on the Long Lake and the last great catch of the season. The Bardings of Dale pack their autumn provisions with the methodical care of people who know winter is a real enemy and preparation is the only weapon against it.
The season turns and Dale counts its autumn tallies. The Bardings have a word for a well-provisioned autumn: ready. They are working toward being ready. The march reflects that.

Harvest and last-fish season around Esgaroth. The Bardings of Dale finish their autumn accounting with the same focused practicality that rebuilt their city from dragon-ash. Numbers can be recovered from. Unpreparedness cannot.

Winter on the Long Lake and the ice comes slowly then all at once. The Bardings of Dale know this — they have wintered beside the Mountain for generations — and their preparations reflect it. They are never quite caught by surprise.
Cold winter at the foot of the Lonely Mountain. The Bardings huddle against the mountain wind and continue their commerce — in Dale, trade does not stop for winter. It adjusts.

The Long Winter descends and the Bardings are, cautiously, prepared. The memory of worse winters lives in Esgaroth — when the lake froze deep and the ice took what the dragon had left. This is not that. This, they can manage.

Three days of Dale at its most prosperous — spring fish, unburdened column, Long Lake running full. The Bardings are doing what they do best: managing abundance as carefully as they manage scarcity. [Sustained Peak]

King Brand's soldiers have held their peak for three days. Fish to surplus, column to clean, march to maximum efficiency — the Bardings of Esgaroth are operating as though the dragon was a story and the rebuilt city is the reality. [Sustained Peak]

Three consecutive days of Dale operating at its potential. The Long Lake is generous and the column is free. Something like the city's old confidence is travelling with these soldiers — the confidence of a people who rebuilt the impossible. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of the worst. Empty barrels and too many captives and a column that is slowing by degrees. The Bardings of Dale keep walking because stopping is not in their character — but the ledger shows three days of loss, and the ledger does not forgive. [Sustained Dire]

The third consecutive day. Dale's soldiers are still moving, still accounting, still noting each shortfall in the column's running tally. Three days of deficit has put the Bardings in a very particular mood: determined, grim, and looking for a correction. [Sustained Dire]

Three days and no recovery. The practical mind of Dale knows what this means — the current approach isn't working. Something must change, and the Bardings of Esgaroth are exactly the kind of people who make changes when the numbers tell them to. [Sustained Dire]

The vegetable sacks are empty and the Hobbits are looking at each other with expressions that range from deeply worried to actively distressed. In the Shire, running out of food is not a supply problem. It is a crisis.

Nothing in the provision packs. The Hobbits of the Shire have never, in all their generations, run out of food on a march — because Hobbits were never meant to be on marches in the first place. This feels like both problems at once.

Three days without proper vegetables and the Shire-folk are not handling it well. They are still walking, still trying, still apologising to the captives for the reduced rations — but they are genuinely, deeply sad about the food.
Garden vegetables from the finest plots in the Westfarthing. The Hobbits have packed well — seven meals a day may be an ambition on campaign, but they have tried their best.
Bag End potatoes and Took-family carrots, distributed at the midday halt. The Shire's soldiers eat with the dedication of a people for whom meals are a sacred institution.
Westfarthing produce unpacked with the reverence the Shire reserves for good food. Even on campaign, a Hobbit's relationship with vegetables is a serious thing.

The provision packs are overflowing with garden vegetables — every Hobbit packed more than was sensible, which means there is more than enough for everyone, including the captives. This is very Hobbit. [Rations: Surplus]

The Shire-folk brought more food than they could possibly need, which was always the plan. Hobbits are not comfortable when there might not be enough, and right now there is definitely enough — and then more. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus garden produce from the best plots in four Farthings. The Hobbits are sharing with everyone, including people who didn't ask, and are visibly happier now that no one is going to go without. This is what the Shire considers crisis preparedness. [Rations: Surplus]
Far too many captives. Hobbits are not built for this — their hearts are too large for prisons, and the column is slowing because no one quite has the heart to march them hard. [Prisoner Burden -3]
The prisoner column has grown to a size that is deeply uncomfortable for Hobbit sensibilities. They are still feeding them. That is both admirable and extremely impractical. [Prisoner Burden -3]
Too many captives for the Shire-folk to manage without distress. The Hobbits are trying their best — which means the captives are probably eating better than the soldiers. [Prisoner Burden -3]
A small number of prisoners walk behind. The Shire-folk keep them well enough — with slightly too much bread and slightly too much concern for their wellbeing.
Captives in the column's care. The Hobbits are managing — though 'managing' in the Shire tradition involves more food and more conversation than most military manuals would recommend.
Prisoners being looked after. The Shire does not do captivity without feeling responsible for it — which makes the Hobbits exceptionally thorough wardens, if slightly inefficient ones.
No prisoners slow the Hobbits — the column is as light as a summer walk to the Green Dragon. There is something almost cheerful about it. [Captive Spoils +3]

The Shire-folk march without the weight of captives today. Every Hobbit step is slightly springier for it — which is saying something for creatures already inclined toward cheerful walking. [Captive Spoils +3]
No chains, no burden, no moral complexity trailing behind the column. The Hobbits are clearly relieved — their faces say 'second breakfast was worth it after all'. [Captive Spoils +3]
Midsummer in the Shire: the gardens are overflowing and the roads are empty of chains. Even far from home, this company has managed to feel something like peace. [Faction Peak]

Summer vegetables in abundance and no prisoners weighing on any Hobbit conscience. This is, by Shire standards, an extremely successful campaign. They are discussing it over second breakfast. [Faction Peak]

Full provision packs and an unburdened march in the best vegetable season. The Hobbits of the Shire are about as content as creatures who were not designed for any of this can possibly be. [Faction Peak]
The vegetable sacks are empty and there are far too many captives for Hobbit hearts to bear comfortably. This is not the kind of adventure the songs back home make it sound like. [Faction Dire]
No vegetables and too many prisoners. The Shire-folk are exhausted, over-responsible, and significantly under-fed. Bilbo never mentioned this part. [Faction Dire]

Empty provision bags and a column full of captives that the Hobbits cannot bring themselves to treat unkindly. It is a very Hobbit kind of disaster — deeply inconvenient and entirely well-intentioned. [Faction Dire]

Spring in the Shire and the gardens are waking up. The Hobbits on campaign are thinking about their plots at home — this is the time when the Westfarthing smells best, and they know it, and they miss it.
The Shire blooms in spring. Even on the road, Hobbits who were born there can feel it — a pull toward green things and good soil and the very specific smell of the Westfarthing in the morning.

Spring comes to the Shire in the soldiers' memories. They know exactly what is happening at home right now — the planting, the first green shoots, the smell of rain on good earth. The road is longer for knowing.

High summer and the Shire gardens are at their finest. The Hobbits on campaign know exactly what they are missing, and they eat their field-rations with the resigned dignity of creatures who understand the difference. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Midsummer in the Shire — the very best time. The provision packs are full of summer vegetables that taste nearly as good as eating them fresh from the garden would, which is not the same as eating them from the garden, but is what the campaign allows. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Summer vegetables from the Shire's finest plots, packed with more care than most armies bring to their entire supply operation. The Hobbits eat well in summer, which is to say: they eat as well as Hobbits require, which is very well indeed. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Harvest time in the Shire and the Hobbits are deeply aware of what they are missing. The great autumn feast — second table, third helpings, neighbours brought in from three doors in each direction — is happening without them. This is painful.

The Shire autumn is when everything is at its most abundant and most comfortable. The Hobbit soldiers are doing the math of what the harvest will be, who they have missed, and how long before they can go back. The math is not comforting.

Autumn provisions from the end-of-harvest surplus. The Hobbits packed the last of the summer garden, which is good, and know there will not be more from the same source, which is less good. They eat carefully and try not to think about the Party Field.

Winter in the Shire is the season of fires and second breakfasts and staying indoors with warm drinks. The Hobbits on campaign are achieving approximately none of these things, which is making winter harder than it usually is.
Cold in the Shire — colder than the Westfarthing usually gets. The Hobbit soldiers are bundled in everything they packed and still think of home fireplaces with a longing that is almost physical.

The Shire winter is supposed to be spent inside, eating, reading, and occasionally looking out the round window at the snow. The current arrangement — being outside, in the snow, with insufficient food — is a significant deviation from this plan.

Three days of the Shire at its most itself — summer vegetables overflowing, no chains on anyone's conscience. The Hobbits have been, against all probability, thriving. They are cautiously discussing whether this constitutes an adventure, and cautiously concluding that it might. [Sustained Peak]

The Shire-folk have sustained three days of genuine abundance and genuine ease. Something about the camp feels almost like the Westfarthing. The Hobbits notice this and find it extremely reassuring. [Sustained Peak]

Three days running of the Shire's particular brand of excellence: everyone fed, no one imprisoned, the march lighter than a summer walk. Bilbo would have recognized this. He would have been surprised, but he would have recognized it. [Sustained Peak]

Three days without food and three days of too many captives and three days of the Hobbits doing something they were specifically not designed for. They are still doing it. The determination of the Shire-folk, when tested, is not a small thing. [Sustained Dire]

The third day. The Hobbits of the Shire have now been on short rations and heavy conscience for three consecutive days — something they did not believe was possible when they started and are increasingly certain must end soon. [Sustained Dire]

Three consecutive days of the worst of it. The Hobbits are still walking, still sharing what little they have, still being extraordinarily kind to everyone including the captives who keep looking confused by the kindness. This is the Shire at its most itself, which is both heartbreaking and rather inspiring. [Sustained Dire]

The fruit is gone. The desert warriors of Harad are marching on heat and pride and nothing else, which in the deep south has historically been enough. But the war-chiefs are watching the count and the count is wrong.

Empty provision pouches in the southern column. The Haradrim endure the desert's indifference better than any other people — they were shaped by it — but even the shaped endure better when they are eating.

Three days without the southern fruit. The Haradrim push on because that is what they do — but the war-chief's calculation is running increasingly negative, and in Harad, a negative calculation has consequences.
Sun-dried fruit of the southern groves — sweet as old blood and twice as sustaining. The Haradrim eat as those who know victory tastes better on a full stomach.
Southern palm fruit, dried in the desert heat and carried in woven pouches. The war-chiefs distribute it before the march — strength for the battle, sweetness for the conqueror.
Harad fruit divided at dawn beneath the war-banner. The desert warriors eat with the quiet focus of people for whom a meal before a battle is a ritual, not just a meal.

The fruit pouches are overloaded — Harad's finest palm grove season packed beyond the march's requirements. The desert warriors eat deeply and the column moves with the confidence of an army that knows it has enough. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus from the southern groves, sweet and plentiful. The Haradrim eat without rationing for the first time this march, and the difference in pace is immediate. A southern army with surplus provision is a southern army at full power. [Rations: Surplus]

Desert abundance: palm fruit beyond the column's ability to consume in a week. The war-chiefs distribute without counting and the Haradrim are, in this moment, the full expression of the south at its most generous. [Rations: Surplus]
The war-pens are full and the southern lords are satisfied. Harad counts wealth in chains as much as gold — and right now the count is excellent. [Captive Spoils +5]
Full pens, pleased war-chiefs, and a tribute column that exceeds the season's expectations. Harad has had good campaigns before — but this one is shaping up to be remembered. [Captive Spoils +5]
The prisoner count is excellent and the southern lords are already planning the tribute distribution. Harad's power grows with every chain — and tonight the chains are many. [Captive Spoils +5]
A respectable haul of prisoners marches south. Harad's war-chiefs acknowledge the tally — not ecstatic, but the column is doing its job. [Prisoners in Column +2]

Captives in hand, moving south at adequate pace. The Haradrim note the tally as they note everything — with the calculating attention of desert people who cannot afford to miscalculate. [Prisoners in Column +2]
The prisoner column meets the war-chief's standard. In Harad's accounting, adequate is not praised — but it is not punished. The march continues. [Prisoners in Column +2]
Empty pens. The southern war-chiefs demand tribute and the tribute is not coming. Haradrim warriors who return empty-handed do not return to honour. [Prisoner Burden -5]
Nothing for the pens. The war-chiefs are watching the tribute column and finding it wanting — in the south, a general who returns with nothing has already lost. [Prisoner Burden -5]
Empty chains in the desert sun. Harad does not forgive empty tribute columns — and the war-chiefs are already beginning to calculate what this failure costs in standing. [Prisoner Burden -5]
The summer sun blazes over Harad and the fruit harvest is exceptional. The pens are full and the war-chiefs are content. The south is doing what the south does. [Faction Peak]
High summer in the deep south: fruit at its peak sweetness, pens at capacity. The Haradrim war-machine is operating as it was designed — and as designed, it is formidable. [Faction Peak]
Full fruit stores and full pens under the desert sun. The war-chiefs of Harad are calculating their tribute with visible satisfaction — a rare sight, worth noting. [Faction Peak]
Spent fruit stores and empty prisoner columns. In the deep south, a general who feeds his army nothing and returns with nothing is not a general for long. [Faction Dire]

No fruit, no captives, and a desert that punishes weakness without ceremony. The Haradrim are beginning to question the campaign in terms that war-chiefs tend to find dangerously direct. [Faction Dire]
Empty provisions and empty tribute in the heat of summer. The war-chiefs of Harad have never been patient with failure — and right now, they are out of patience and out of fruit. [Faction Dire]
Spring in the deep south — the desert blooms briefly and the Haradrim feel it as an opening. The campaign routes that the winter dust-storms made impassable clear in spring's mild weeks.
The desert spring: flowers that last a fortnight, then heat. The Haradrim use the brief mild season for the longest marches of the year — distance costs least when the sun is not yet fully committed.
Spring in Harad is a gift that the desert gives and takes back within a month. The war-chiefs move their armies during the gift and plan for the taking-back. This is the southern way.

High summer and the southern sun is absolute. The Haradrim are built for this — fruit at peak, heat at peak, warriors at peak. The desert in full summer is Harad's war-season and the column knows it. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Midsummer in the deep south. The palm groves are heavy and the war-chiefs are at full strength. This is when the south campaigns and this is what it looks like at the height of that. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

The summer sun blazes over everything and the Haradrim march straight into it, because that is what Harad's warriors do. Full fruit, full heat, full army. The south at its most itself. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Autumn in the desert — the heat eases and the trade routes open. The Haradrim begin the autumn accounting: what was taken, what was spent, what must be delivered. The numbers are being made.
The desert cools slightly in autumn and the Haradrim take stock. The season of reckoning — tribute counted, campaign losses recorded, next year's plans beginning to form in the war-chiefs' thinking.
Autumn provisioning from the last of the grove harvest. The Haradrim pack carefully, count carefully, and march on — autumn in the south is practical season, not comfortable season.
