Winter in the deep south — thin by northern standards, cold by Haradrim standards. The war-chiefs reduce the march pace slightly and the column pulls on heavier robes. This is the concession the desert winter gets.

The cool season in Harad. The Haradrim acknowledge it exists and adjust accordingly — slower, more deliberate, with slightly more attention to provision than the hot months require. Not hardship. Just different.

Cold season by Harad's calendar. The southern warriors manage winter with the practical competence of people who have never needed to learn actual survival — this is not actual cold, this is just the absence of excessive heat.

Three days of the south at its maximum. Summer fruit, full pens, and the desert at peak generosity. The Haradrim war-chiefs have been satisfied for three consecutive days — a condition that, in Harad, creates its own kind of legend. [Sustained Peak]

The southern army has held its peak for three days. The desert is being generous and the campaign is being rewarded. War-chiefs who produce three-day peaks in Harad are remembered. These soldiers will be part of that memory. [Sustained Peak]

Three days running of Harad at the height of its power. Full fruit, full tribute, full summer sun. The war-chiefs are letting themselves believe the season is exceptional. Three days says it might be right. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of the south at its worst. The desert is taking rather than giving and the tribute column is empty and the war-chiefs are looking at the general with the specific attention of people calculating alternatives. [Sustained Dire]

The third day. The Haradrim have been on short provision and empty tribute for three days, and in the deep south, three days of failure is enough for the accounting to turn very dark. [Sustained Dire]

Three consecutive days of shortfall. The desert does not forgive sustained weakness, and neither do the Haradrim war-chiefs. Something is going to change at the end of this stretch — the only question is what the change is directed at. [Sustained Dire]
The meat is gone and the Dunlendings are eating bark again, which is what they have always eaten when the kills failed. The hill-folk are built for scarcity. That does not make it less bitter.
Nothing in the Dunlending provision sacks. The wild-men of the Westmarch are used to nothing — every generation was raised on it — but the emptiness sits harder when there are battles ahead.

Three days since the last kill. The hill-chieftains are not saying anything about it, which means they are thinking about it constantly. In Dunland, the things that are not said are usually the most dangerous.
Gristled plainsmeat, torn raw from the bone and divided without ceremony. The Wildmen of Dunland have always eaten this way — and they have always survived.
Hill-kill, barely cooled from the chase, divided by the chieftain without words. The wild-men of the Westmarch do not wait to be fed — they take what the hills give and keep moving.
Raw meat from the last hunt passed hand to hand in the dark. The Dunlendings eat as their ancestors ate — fast, rough, and with no illusions about what they are.

The kill was exceptional and the Dunlending provision is overflowing for the first time in anyone's recent memory. The wild-men eat with the focused intensity of creatures who know surplus is temporary and should be consumed accordingly. [Rations: Surplus]

More meat than the hill-folk have seen in a single haul in living memory. The Dunlendings eat without counting for once, and the column moves with an unusual lightness — the lightness of creatures that, for this one day, have enough. [Rations: Surplus]

Surplus kill from the finest hunt the Westmarch has produced this season. The Dunlendings eat deeply and move harder. The chieftain watches the surplus with deep suspicion — in his experience, this much good fortune means something bad is approaching. [Rations: Surplus]
Captives drag behind the Wildmen's column — spoils to flaunt before the other hill-chieftains. Dunland measures power in what it has taken, and right now the taking is good. [Captive Spoils +5]

Full chains behind the Dunlending column. The hill-chieftains are counting their prizes with the grim satisfaction of people for whom conquest is both profession and personal score-settling. [Captive Spoils +5]

The war-band brings home captives and the chieftain's authority grows with every chain. Dunland power is demonstrated, not explained — and right now it is being demonstrated in force. [Captive Spoils +5]
A useful number of prisoners for a Dunland war-band of this size. The hill-folk move on with the quiet satisfaction of men who are not disappointed. [Prisoners in Column +2]
Captives in hand, march proceeding. The wild-men note the tally and find it neither insufficient nor inspiring. They move on.
The prisoner escort is manageable. Dunland war-bands do not have excessive feelings about adequate performance — they just keep walking.

Empty chains behind the column. The Wildmen came down from the hills for plunder and have found none. A Dunlending chieftain with nothing to show is a chieftain whose authority is slipping. [Prisoner Burden -5]
No captives. No spoils. The hill-chieftain is looking at the empty chains with the expression of a man calculating exactly how much authority he has lost today. [Prisoner Burden -5]
The war-band returns with nothing to show the other chieftains. In Dunland, empty hands are a political statement — and not a favourable one. [Prisoner Burden -5]

Deep winter and the meat is plentiful. The prisoner column is long. The Wildmen of Dunland are in their element — cold, brutal, and satisfied in the way only those who expect very little can be. [Faction Peak]
Winter cold, full meat, full chains. The Dunlendings are operating as their hills made them — hard, hungry for results, and currently getting them. [Faction Peak]
The worst season and the best campaign. The wild-men of the Westmarch have meat in hand and captives in chains — which is, for them, as close to prosperity as the hills allow. [Faction Peak]

The meat is gone and the chains are empty. The hill-chieftains are looking at each other across the fire with the measuring looks that precede a change of leadership. In Dunland, those changes are rarely peaceful. [Faction Dire]

No meat, no captives, deep winter. The wild-men of Dunland are hungry and empty-handed — a combination that historically produces either very good or very bad results, depending entirely on who is standing closest to the chieftain. [Faction Dire]
Bare racks and bare chains in the worst of the winter cold. The hill-folk are looking for someone to blame — and in Dunland, that search is always brief and always has the same ending. [Faction Dire]

Spring thaws the hills and the Dunlendings come out of their winter shelters with the specific energy of people whose grievances have been building since autumn. The hill-folk are moving and they know exactly where they are moving toward.
The Westmarch greens up in spring and the war-bands form. The Dunlendings measure their spring by how many have survived the winter and how much they are owed by those who made the winter necessary.

Spring in Dunland — the season of old scores reopened and new ones added to the tally. The wild-men of the hills move with the focused purposefulness of people who have been waiting all winter to move.

High summer in the hills and the root harvest is coming in. The Dunlendings are briefly, cautiously, adequately fed — a condition they meet with the suspicious pragmatism of people who have learned not to trust abundance. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Midsummer in the Westmarch. The hill-folk eat what the summer gives and move harder for it. Dunland in summer is as close to contented as Dunland gets — which is not content, but is less actively resentful. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Summer provision in the Dunland hills. The roots are up and the meat is there and the column is moving with an energy that the lean months never quite permit. The wild-men take what the season offers and ask no questions about why it was offered. [Peak Season Bonus Active]
Autumn in the Westmarch — the stores are packed and the Dunlendings begin their annual calculation of how little the winter will leave them. The answer is usually: less than they started with.

The hills turn brown in autumn and the hill-folk pull back toward their winter shelters. The Dunlendings use the last good weeks of the year to take whatever the season's campaign has produced, and count it against the grievances it cost them.

Autumn in Dunland is the season of counting. The wild-men count their kills, count their captives, count their losses, and decide whether the balance justifies winter. It rarely does. They plan to do better next spring.

Deep winter in the Westmarch hills and the cold is an old enemy that the Dunlendings know intimately. They hunker in their hill-shelters with the focused resentment of people who have survived this before and will survive it again. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Winter cold in the hills of Dunland. The wild-men know this cold the way they know everything about their hard homeland — with exact, practical knowledge and zero illusions. The meat is there and the cold is there and they manage both. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

The Dunland winter. The hill-folk of the Westmarch were shaped by this — by cold and scarcity and the kind of endurance that has no name because naming it would take energy they don't have. They survive it. They always survive it. [Peak Season Bonus Active]

Three days of the Westmarch at its impossible best. Meat, captives, winter cold — the Dunlendings are operating at a peak they have not maintained in living memory. The chieftains are not talking about it, because talking about it would be tempting something. [Sustained Peak]

The hill-folk have held their peak for three days. For Dunland, this is not just exceptional — it is historically unusual. Three days of having enough and taking enough is something the Westmarch songs will eventually describe. [Sustained Peak]

Three consecutive days of Dunland winning. The hill-chieftains are grimly satisfied in the specific way of people who have waited their entire lives for three consecutive winning days and are not entirely sure what to do with them. [Sustained Peak]

Three days of the worst. The Dunlendings are marching on pure grudge now — no food, no spoils, nothing but the hill-folk stubbornness that has sustained them through a thousand winters of exactly this. [Sustained Dire]

The third day running. Empty provisions and empty chains — the specific combination that in Dunland means the chieftain's authority is being actively questioned. Not yet loudly. Not yet. [Sustained Dire]

Three consecutive days of nothing. The hill-folk of the Westmarch have always had nothing — they were born to nothing, raised on nothing, and the valley people made certain nothing was what they kept. Three more days of this and nothing becomes something that moves. [Sustained Dire]
{HERO} leads this column. The soldiers know the name and what it means — there is a steadiness in the ranks that comes from following someone the songs have already started writing about.
With {HERO} at the head of this march, something shifts in the column's bearing. The men stand differently when the right person is leading them.
{HERO} is here. For the soldiers of this company, that single fact does more for morale than a week of good provisions.
Your general's nature is not entirely hidden. The men follow, because honour demands it — but the demands of honour are being tested by proximity to something they do not entirely trust.
There is a darkness in your commander that the good soldiers of this host feel without being able to name. It does not break them. But it troubles the march.
An ill-aligned leader among good soldiers. The company follows because duty requires it. Duty, in this case, is working harder than it should have to.
Your general carries the honour of a good people among soldiers bred for darkness. The men respect it less than they fear it — but both are noted.
There is something in your bearing that sits uneasily with these ranks. The soldiers serve, because that is what they do — but they are watching the gap between what you believe and what they are.
A good-hearted commander among evil soldiers. The tension is not spoken. It does not need to be. It rides in every order given and every order followed.

Haradrim war-chiefs have brought their soldiers into your host. They march to their own rhythm — the desert rhythm, which is different from yours, faster in some ways and with different stopping points.

A southern contingent is in your army. The Haradrim sustain themselves on their own fruit and their own pride, both of which they have in considerable quantity. They are allies of convenience. Effective ones.

The warriors of Harad march in your host. Their culture's morale system is not your culture's morale system — they measure different things and find satisfaction in different results. The combined army benefits from both.

Variags from Khand march in your host. Professional, contractual, and entirely transactional. They maintain their own accounts, eat their cheese, and will fight precisely as contracted. Not a soldier more.
A Khand mercenary contingent is in your army. They are here because they are being paid the agreed rate. They will leave if the rate changes. Right now the rate is being paid and the column benefits.

The Variags are in your column today. They separate their provisions, their morale system, and their sense of professional obligation from yours entirely. This is a business arrangement and they treat it as one.

Bardings from Dale march in your host. Practical, organised, and slightly baffled by anything that isn't a straightforward transaction or a straightforward fight. They are provisioned, present, and useful.
A company from Esgaroth has joined the march. They bring their own smoke-fish, their own ledgers, and their own pragmatic approach to being alive. Good soldiers. Reliable allies.

Dale's contingent is in your army. They manage their provisions with the same efficiency they bring to market trading, and they fight with the same determination they brought to rebuilding their city. Both qualities are welcome.
Hunters from Dol Guldur have joined your march. They move through the column like shadow — barely visible, entirely present, and sustained by something you'd rather not examine too closely.

The shadow-soldiers of the old fortress are in your host. They sustain themselves on the Necromancer's power as much as on provisions. Their morale is not a human system and should not be measured as one.
Dol Guldur's creatures march in your army. The other soldiers give them space. The space is generous. The dark contingent doesn't notice — or, if it does, prefers it.

Hill-folk from Dunland have joined your march. They keep to themselves, eat what they brought, and maintain a careful neutrality toward your soldiers that is the hill-folk version of polite. It is better than the alternative.

A Dunlending contingent is in your host. Wild-men from the Westmarch, marching with your column for reasons that probably have more to do with who else is involved than with who you are. They fight. That's enough.

The hill-folk are in your army. They watch your soldiers with the measuring look of people who are adding everything up and not sharing the total. They are useful allies and uncomfortable company, which is exactly what the Dunlendings always are.

Dunlending hill-folk march with your host. They keep apart from the main column, eat what they brought from their own hills, and watch your soldiers with the suspicious patience of people who have never trusted valley-folk and see no reason to start now.
A contingent of Dunland wild-men is in your army. They fight well and require little — that is the extent of what they wish to be known for. Their morale is their own business.
Hill-folk from the Westmarch march in your host. They keep their own pace, eat their own provisions, and maintain the specific distance of allies who remember every reason they shouldn't be allies.

Dwarves from Erebor march in your host. They keep their own rations, carry their own axes, and maintain their own extremely specific opinions about how a camp should be organised. They are formidable allies.
A Dwarven contingent from the Lonely Mountain has joined the march. They eat Cram, complain about nothing, and move slower than cavalry and faster than they look. Excellent company in a tight place.
Erebor's soldiers are in your column. They are self-sufficient, unambiguous about their preferences, and entirely reliable. They expect to be treated as equals. They are.
A contingent from the White City marches in your host. The Men of Gondor keep their own counsel, maintain their own rations, and measure morale by their own standards. Two armies share a road.
Gondor's soldiers ride with you today. They eat their own provisions and sing their own songs at night — the two cultures march together, but the march has two different hearts.
The silver and black of Gondor moves beside your colours. The soldiers acknowledge each other with the careful courtesy of people who respect what they don't entirely understand.

Gundabad Orcs march in your host. The mountain soldiers keep their own formation, eat what they have, and make no particular effort to be liked. They are here because they are being paid or commanded. They will fight.
A mountain Orc contingent from Gundabad is in your army. They are not enthusiastic allies. They are functional ones. Your soldiers maintain a prudent personal space.
The Orcs of Gundabad march with you. They know the passes better than any other contingent and care about your cause less than any other contingent. Both facts are useful in different circumstances.

Southern warriors from Harad march in your host. They sustain themselves on desert fruit and desert pride, keep their own formation, and maintain the composure of people who have survived conditions that would end most other armies.
A Haradrim contingent is in your army. They are used to conditions that would break a northern army — the combined host is harder for having them in it.

The warriors of the deep south march with your column. They eat their own provisions, follow their own war-chief, and measure success in the southern way. The alliance is practical and, on both sides, entirely calculated.

Uruk-hai from Isengard march in your host. They eat raw, sleep little, and do not particularly care about your cause. They care about orders and results. Right now your orders and their results coincide.
Saruman's soldiers are in your column. Effective, unsentimental, and professionally indifferent to everything except the task. They are not friends. They are not enemies. They are useful.
Isengard's Uruks are here. Your soldiers eye them. The Uruks eye your soldiers. The march proceeds. When the fighting starts, all of that becomes irrelevant.

Easterling warriors march in your host. Dragon-helm soldiers, bred for the eastern tribute campaigns, moving alongside your column with the quiet efficiency of people doing a job they have been trained for since childhood.

A contingent of Rhûn's warriors is in your army. They follow their own cultural protocols, sustain themselves on their own salt-meat, and measure success by eastern tribute standards. The combined host is larger and more capable.

The Easterlings are in your march. They are professional, proven, and not particularly interested in your reasons for being here. They are interested in the campaign producing results. Ensure it does.

The Galadhrim march with your host. They are gracious, capable, and slightly beyond the concerns of ordinary armies — their lembas, their silence, and their particular sadness travel with them. The column is honoured by their presence.

Soldiers from Lothlórien are in your army. They sustain themselves on their own provisions and their own resolve, which are both, by all evidence, considerable. They maintain a respectful distance that feels like grace rather than coldness.
The Golden Wood's warriors are here. They are allies in the full sense — but their morale runs on deeper channels than yours, and you would not wish to interfere with those channels.

Wood-elves from Mirkwood have joined your march. They move like smoke through your formations — there, then not quite there — and they sustain themselves on Dorwinion vintage and the particular stubbornness of forest creatures.
The Silvan Elves are in your host. They do not eat your provisions. They do not sleep in your camp. They do fight in your battles — and when they do, you remember why you wanted them.
A contingent of Mirkwood's warriors shadows your column. Literally shadows it. They are useful, present when needed, and impossible to fully account for.
Mordor's soldiers march in your host. They follow orders because orders come with consequences, not because they believe in your cause. They are effective and deeply uncomfortable company.
A contingent from the Black Land moves with your column. Their morale runs on different fuel than yours — darker fuel, and less subject to the things you use to maintain yours. Useful. Unsettling.

Sauron's soldiers are in your army today. The column is stronger for them and stranger for them simultaneously. Their presence is noted. Their motivations are separate from yours and should stay that way.

The Noldor of Rivendell march in your host. Their lembas sustains them beyond mortal measure and their composure is, frankly, a little unsettling. They are not unfriendly. They are simply not entirely present in the same way you are.

Elven soldiers from Imladris move with your column — serene, unhurried, and fundamentally elsewhere even when standing beside you. Their morale is its own system. It is also, by any measure, excellent.

Rivendell's company marches in your host. The Noldor eat their own provisions, keep their own counsel, and occasionally say things that make you think they know how this ends. They are, regardless, valuable allies.

Riders of the Mark march with your host. They keep apart, set their own camp, and follow the cavalry's restless need to be moving at all times. The column is faster for having them and harder to organise.

Rohirric cavalry are in your army. They will not slow to your pace, they will not eat your provisions, and they will not pretend the alliance is warmer than it is. They will fight when the horn sounds.

The Riddermark's soldiers are here. They ride their own pace, eat their own grain, and measure the day in horse-lengths rather than miles. The column benefits from their presence in ways that are hard to count and easy to feel.

Hobbits from the Shire are marching in your host. They packed enough food for twice the journey, have offered some to everyone, and are maintaining an admirable courage that doesn't quite hide the fact that they are deeply, sincerely terrified.

A Shire company is in your army. They are thoroughly out of their element, thoroughly determined to be useful anyway, and keeping morale up by sharing provisions with everyone within reach. Remarkable creatures.

The Shire-folk are here, improbably. Their morale is their own — which is to say, it is fuelled by stubbornness, homesickness, and a truly extraordinary quantity of packed vegetables. They are not giving up.

The Bardings of Dale have attached their company to your march. They manage their provisions with the practical efficiency of lake-traders, and their morale runs on fish and fair dealing rather than whatever yours runs on.
A contingent from Esgaroth marches with your host. Practical, disciplined, and slightly suspicious of non-traders. Their morale is their own affair — and their affairs are, as always, in order.
Dale's soldiers are in your column today. They keep separate ledgers, separate rations, and separate opinions. They'll fight when it counts.
Corsairs from Umbar have attached their company to your host. They are here for pay, plunder, or both. Their loyalty is transactional and their morale runs on profit. Make sure the profit is present.

The Corsairs of Umbar march with your column. They are experienced fighters and experienced negotiators. Right now they are being paid to be the former. Be careful not to accidentally trigger the latter.

Umbarian sailors are in your army — slightly confused by the absence of a ship, but adapting. They manage their own provisions, manage their own morale, and will leave if the arrangement stops being profitable.
The Riders of the Mark are in your host. They set their own camp, eat their own grain, and trust their horses more than your formation orders. They fight well regardless.
Rohirric outriders move on your flanks — a different culture, a different pace, a different relationship with hunger and speed. The combined army is stronger for them, even if less unified.
Rohan rides with you. The Riders don't quite march — they move in that Rohirric way that isn't quite cavalry and isn't quite infantry and is entirely itself. The column is better for having them.
Desert terrain — the Haradrim are exactly where they belong. The heat that punishes other armies is simply the temperature to these soldiers. The column moves at full speed.
Sand and sun and the specific silence of the deep desert. The Haradrim are in their element — the column moves with the easy mastery of creatures that were shaped by this landscape.
Desert country. The Haradrim don't slow in the heat. They accelerate. This is what they were born into, trained in, and built for. The desert is not an obstacle. It is home.

Open steppe country — the Variags of Khand recognise this terrain. The great plains require different skills than the Westmarch hills or the mountain passes, and Khand's mercenaries have those skills.

Steppe and open plain — the Variags are on familiar ground. They move across it with the practiced efficiency of people who have spent their professional lives calculating the most efficient route across exactly this.
The high plateau country that reminds the Variags of Khand. They read this terrain in terms of operational range and supply logistics. Both, here, are favourable.
The Long Lake country — the Bardings are on familiar ground. The roads near Esgaroth are known to Dale's soldiers; they know which fords are safe and which inns are worth stopping at.
Lake and river country near Dale. The Bardings move through it with the familiar efficiency of people who have made these roads profitable for generations.
The plains near the Lonely Mountain. Dale's soldiers know this country — the routes, the distances, the landmarks. The march is easier on ground you have walked before.
Old forest — the kind that Dol Guldur's hunters know. The darkness is thicker here, the paths less certain. The shadow-soldiers move through it with the ease of creatures that live in exactly this.
Deep forest around the column, old and dark and exactly like Mirkwood's worst places. The creatures of the old fortress are at home here. The shadow deepens around them.
Ancient woodland, the kind where the light doesn't reach the ground. The hunters of Dol Guldur move through it like they are part of it — which, in a sense, they are.
The Westmarch hills — Dunlending country. The wild-men know every slope of this terrain; they were born hiding in it and raised making war from it.
Hill terrain, steep and familiar. The Dunlendings move through it at twice the pace of the main column, on paths that aren't on any map and have no names except the ones they gave them.
The old hills of Dunland. The column moves through terrain that the hill-folk have fought over, hidden in, and survived on for generations. Every rock is known. Every path is remembered.
The Western hills — Dunlending country. The wild-men of the Westmarch are on their own ground and the difference is immediate. They move faster and quieter and with a great deal less uncertainty.
Hill terrain, steep and familiar. The Dunlendings know every fold of this ground — where to watch, where to move fast, where the path that isn't marked is better than the path that is.
The Westmarch hills. Home ground for the wild-men of Dunland, and home ground changes everything. The column moves with the specific confidence of people who know exactly where they are.
Mountain terrain — and the Dwarves of Erebor are home. The passes that slow other armies are nothing to the sons of Durin, who walk rock the way the Rohirrim walk grass.
The high stone of the mountains is beneath the Dwarven column and the difference is immediate. The Dwarves of Erebor are faster in mountains than they are anywhere else. The mountain knows them.

Rock and height — the Dwarves are exactly where they belong. Erebor's soldiers move through the mountain terrain with the ease of people who spent their lives underground and never found anything better.
The plains around Minas Tirith — familiar ground to the soldiers of the White City. The column moves with the easy confidence of an army that knows every contour of the land it's defending.
Gondorian country. The soldiers breathe differently here — the specific ease of people who know the names of the farms they're passing and the families inside them.
The rolling plains of Gondor beneath the column's feet. The men of the White City march on their own soil and they know it. It shows in everything from the pace to the posture.
The high passes of the Misty Mountains. Gundabad's Orcs are in the terrain they were born in — the column moves through rock and snow with the ease of creatures that never needed a path to find one.
Mountain snow and deep passes — Gundabad's home ground. The warlords move faster here than anywhere else, in the cold dark of the highest passes where no other army would follow.
The mountain fortress country. Gundabad's soldiers are exactly where they are most dangerous — on their own peaks, in their own cold, moving through terrain that kills the unprepared.
Desert country — proper desert, the kind the Haradrim were born into. The heat is absolute and the column is at full capacity. This is not hardship. This is home.
Sand and sun and the deep silence of the true desert. The warriors of Harad move through it with the authority of people for whom this landscape is the only one that ever fully made sense.
The desert in full summer heat. The Haradrim don't notice. They are home, and home, for the people of Harad, has always been exactly this extreme.
Mountain terrain near the Wizard's Vale. The Uruks of Isengard know these passes — they were bred to hold them and raid from them. The column moves at maximum efficiency.
The mountain country around Isengard. The White Hand's soldiers are on their operational home ground — the terrain that Saruman chose specifically because his creatures know it best.
Stone and height near the Wizard's Vale. The Uruk-hai move through it the way they move through everything — without grace, without hesitation, and with terrible effectiveness.
Eastern plains — the Easterlings are on their own ground. The steppe that the Dragon-helm's soldiers were trained to campaign across opens before the column, and the pace accelerates.

Steppe country east of the mountains. The Easterlings read this terrain like text — every feature of it carries tactical meaning that their generations of campaigning here have encoded into the culture.
The great eastern plains. The Dragon-helm's warriors move across them with the ease of creatures bred for exactly this — long marches, open ground, the horizon as the only limit.
Forest light filtering through old trees. The Galadhrim are in landscape that their hearts understand — the column moves with a grace that the open roads never quite permitted.
Deep forest around the column, and the Galadhrim find something like peace in it. Not the Golden Wood's specific golden light — but enough forest, deep enough, that the soldiers breathe easier.
The great trees close around the march and the Galadhrim step lighter. This is the kind of country the Lady's people were made for — canopy, root, the slow patient life of old wood.
Forest country — old, deep, and known to the wood-elves of Mirkwood down to every root and hollow. The Silvan Elves move through it like water through rock, finding the paths that aren't paths.
The great forest closes around the column and the wood-elves are suddenly entirely themselves. Whatever discomfort they carried on open roads vanishes the moment the canopy closes overhead.
Mirkwood — or country enough like it that the Silvan Elves are at home. They move differently in the forest. Faster. Quieter. Like the trees are allies rather than obstacles.
Ash and rock — the terrain of the Black Land. Mordor's soldiers are exactly where they belong. The volcanic ground is hostile to everything that isn't them and they know it.
Mountain and ash-plain — this is Mordor's landscape, and its soldiers move through it with the ease of creatures made for exactly this. The rock is familiar. The darkness is home.
The black mountains and ash-plains of Mordor beneath the column. The servants of the Dark Lord move faster on their own ground — faster and darker and harder to stop.

Mountain approaches that the Noldor recognise. The hidden valley is not far. The Elvish column moves through the high passes with the ease of people for whom this landscape is not hostile geography but memory.

The mountain paths around Rivendell — the Noldor know these routes better than anyone alive, and better than most things that have ever lived. The column moves through difficult terrain as if it were a garden path.
The high country near Imladris. The Noldor are in the landscape they were built for — waterfalls, hidden paths, the specific high-altitude air that seems to carry something more than just oxygen.
The plains of the Riddermark — the Rohirrim are at home. The horses feel the grass change under their hooves and they run differently on good ground. The whole column lifts.
Open Rohirric country. The Riders of the Mark are on the plains they were born to ride, and the difference from road-march to home-ground is felt in every hoofbeat.
The Wold and the Eastemnet and the smell of the Riddermark's grass. The Rohirrim don't slow here — they open up. This is what the Mark was made for.
Gentle hills and green lanes — not quite the Westfarthing, but close enough that the Hobbits feel the kinship. The column moves with a small but real lightening of heart.
Pastoral country — the kind of country the Shire is built on. The Hobbits are not home, but they are in country that reminds them of home, and that is enough to make the road slightly shorter.
Green hills and quiet roads. The Shire-folk feel something familiar in this terrain — a recognition that makes the campaign feel marginally less impossible than it did yesterday.
The roads near Esgaroth — the column recognises the country. The Bardings of Dale are on familiar ground, and familiar ground is the best ground.
Lake-country. The Bardings breathe easier near the Long Lake — the sound of water, the smell of smoke-fish on the wind, the feeling that the road knows them.
The plains around Dale. Home territory for the Bardings, and the difference is visible in the way the scouts move — confident, reading the land the way they read their own ledgers.
Coastal plain — country the Corsairs of Umbar understand. The smell of salt air doesn't reach this far inland, but the flat ground and the sight-lines remind the sailors of the bay.
Open coastal terrain that reminds the Umbarian soldiers of home. They move with the alert, transactional confidence of people who have scouted these routes before for different purposes.
The flat lands near the coast. The Corsairs of Umbar are more comfortable here than in the mountains — they can see threats coming, plan their exits, and calculate the distance to the nearest port.
The open plains of the Riddermark stretch to the horizon — horse country, the only country the Rohirrim have ever truly needed. The column moves like a wave on the grass.
Riddermark plains beneath Rohirric hooves. The horses are glad to be here — the men are glad to see the horses glad. Everything moves easier in the Eastfold.
The Wold opens up ahead. The Riders of the Mark are on their own ground and it shows — heads higher, strides longer, the specific ease of creatures exactly where they belong.

Mountain terrain. The Haradrim are in cold, rocky country far from the desert warmth that sustains them. The cold is genuine hardship for desert warriors — the column slows and the soldiers pull their robes tight.
The high passes are hostile to the desert warriors of Harad. Cold, narrow, with no sight of the sun they were built under. The Haradrim endure it with grim southern determination.
Forest and mountain — the most alien terrain the warriors of Harad can find themselves in. No desert horizon, no palm-grove smell, no familiar heat. The march continues, but at cost.
Forest terrain. The Variags of Khand are steppe people — the closed-in world of old forest doesn't suit their operational style or their sightlines. The column moves more cautiously than it should.

Dense forest. The mercenaries from Khand are used to open country where threats can be seen coming. The forest removes that advantage and the Variags don't like it — professionally, operationally, and existentially.
Old woodland. The Variags function in every terrain because they are professionals — but the forest costs them the sightlines they depend on, and the cost shows in the pace.
Desert terrain. The hunters of Dol Guldur are shadow-creatures — the bright desert light is hostile to them in ways that go beyond temperature. The column moves, but the shadow is thin here.
Open desert and full sun. The creatures of the old fortress are at their most diminished in this light — the shadow that sustains them is thinnest in the desert, under a sky that offers no canopy.
The desert is anti-terrain for the shadow of Dol Guldur. The hunters move through it, because they always move through obstacles — but the power that feeds them is reduced here, and they feel it.

Desert terrain. The hill-folk of Dunland are entirely out of their element — no hills, no cover, no familiar cold. The column moves through the heat with the grim persistence of people who have no good option.
Open desert — no hills, no shelter, nothing that resembles the Westmarch in any way. The Dunlendings push through it the way they push through everything: badly and successfully.

Sand and sun and the complete absence of a hill to retreat to. The hill-folk are in the worst possible terrain for their particular brand of fighting. They continue anyway. That's all that can be said.

Desert terrain — the Dunlendings are far from their hills. The open, flat, treeless heat is as alien to the hill-folk as anything could be. The column moves, but the wild-men are watching the horizon for familiar silhouettes that aren't coming.
The desert is everything the Westmarch hills are not. The Dunlendings move through it as they move through everything they dislike — with grudging persistence and impressive endurance.
Hill-folk in desert country. No cover, no familiar paths, no hills to retreat to. The Dunlendings are uncomfortable and moving quickly, which is the hill-folk version of admitting to a problem.

Forest terrain — the Dwarves of Erebor find it oppressive in ways they can't fully articulate. Too many living things in too many directions. Not enough stone. The column moves, but less confidently than it would in rock.

Deep forest. The sons of Durin were made for stone, not wood. The trees are unfamiliar obstacles and the roots are unfamiliar hazards. The Dwarves endure it with stoic determination and obvious preference for elsewhere.
The Dwarven column moves through forest terrain with the careful competence of people doing something they were not built for and know it. They will manage. They will also not forget.
Mountain terrain — not the country the White City's soldiers were built for. The column moves carefully through passes that Gondorian captains know from maps but not from bones.

The high passes and mountain roads test Gondorian logistics in ways the plains don't. The soldiers of the White City endure it — endurance is a Gondorian virtue — but the march is slower than it should be.
Gondor's soldiers are a long way from the Pelennor. Mountain country is not their country, and the difference in pace tells the whole story.

Desert terrain. The mountain Orcs are far from the cold passes where they belong — the heat is wrong, the light is wrong, and the ground doesn't have enough rock in it. The column keeps moving because it must.
The desert. Gundabad's soldiers are in the worst possible terrain for creatures shaped by mountain cold. They endure it because Orcs endure everything. But they do not endure it well.
Sand and sun — the antithesis of Gundabad's mountain fortress. The warlords push the column forward through sheer force of Orcish persistence. The persistence is remarkable. The efficiency is not.

Mountain terrain. The desert warriors of Harad are in the cold heights — the worst terrain for people shaped by desert heat. The column slows, the soldiers pull their heavier robes on, and the war-chiefs do not look pleased.
Forest and mountain country. The Haradrim are far from the sun they need. The cold of the high country is an actual hazard for people for whom winter in the deep south is a mild inconvenience.
The mountains are the antithesis of Harad. The Haradrim endure them because desert warriors endure everything — but the endurance is costly, and the war-chiefs are counting the cost.
The open desert is far from the Wizard's Vale. The Uruk-hai are built for mountain and cold — the heat is inefficient in ways Saruman would find irritating to calculate.
Desert terrain. Isengard's industrial logic doesn't account well for extreme heat — the Uruks function, because they always function, but at reduced effectiveness that the White Wizard would note.
Sand and sun. The Uruk-hai were made for cold mountain work, not desert campaigning. They continue. Everything about Isengard continues. But something is off by a measurable degree.

Forest terrain — the Easterlings are east-plain people. The forest removes the cavalry advantage that eastern campaigning is built around. The Dragon-helm's soldiers move through it effectively but without joy.

Dense woodland. The eastern warriors are in terrain that reduces the advantages they were trained to exploit. They adapt, because the Dragon-helm's armies are adaptable, but forest campaigning is not what they came for.
The closed forest is not the open steppe. The Easterlings note the terrain as a professional challenge and adjust their formations accordingly. The adjustment costs something.

The arid lands — the Galadhrim find them beautiful and alien simultaneously. Far from the forest and far from the Lady's light, the soldiers of Lothlórien march through terrain that offers no comfort of familiarity.
Desert country. The Golden Wood's soldiers are graceful in alien terrain, but the grace is achieved rather than natural. Every step away from the forest is a step further from what they are.
The Galadhrim in the desert. The contrast with Lothlórien is absolute — and the soldiers feel it, even as they march perfectly, because Elves feel everything perfectly.

The desert is as hostile to the wood-elves as any terrain could be. No forest, no shade, no life that they recognise. The Silvan Elves move through it in the specific misery of creatures far from their element.
Desert terrain — the Silvan Elves find it hostile in a way that mountain or plain never quite manages to be. Something in the absence of forest makes the wood-elves less themselves.
Open desert. The wood-elves are performing a forced march through the landscape they are least equipped to endure. They will endure it. They will not enjoy it.
Forest terrain — the servants of the Dark Lord find the living wood disconcerting. Mordor was built for ash and stone. The green and growing things here carry a light that the shadow doesn't welcome.
Deep forest. The creatures of Mordor move through it with the specific unease of things that belong in darkness and are being asked to move through a world where the light finds them.
Old forest. Not Mirkwood, not Fangorn — but forest enough that the Mordor column is less effective here than in the mountain and ash country it was made for.

Desert terrain — the Noldor find this landscape beautiful and exhausting simultaneously. The dry heat is antithetical to everything Rivendell stands for, and the Elves feel it in ways they would not describe as mere physical discomfort.
The arid lands are far from Imladris in every sense. The Noldor are graceful in alien terrain, as they are graceful in everything, but the grace costs more here than it would at home.
The Noldor in desert country. They manage it perfectly, because they manage everything perfectly — but the waterfalls of Rivendell are very far away right now, and the distance is felt.

Mountain terrain. The Shire-folk are genuinely alarmed by the height. The paths are narrow, the drops are significant, and none of this was in the songs about adventures. The Hobbits are managing. Barely.
High mountain passes. The Hobbits were not built for this — their feet, which are designed for pleasant country lanes, are performing heroically in terrain they were not designed for.

Rocky mountain country far above anything the Westfarthing ever prepared the Hobbits for. They are still walking. They are walking while making very specific small noises of distress that they are pretending no one can hear.
Desert terrain — no lakes, no fish, no familiar landmarks. The Bardings of Dale are well outside their operational range and they know it. The ledger shows it.
The heat and dust of desert country is foreign to the Long Lake people. Dale's soldiers push through it with the practical stubbornness of people who know that complaining changes nothing.
Sand and sun and the complete absence of anything that smells like Esgaroth. The Bardings of Dale are marching through terrain they did not train for, and the march reflects it.

Mountain and snow — the Corsairs of Umbar are as far from the Bay of Belfalas as they have ever been. The height is wrong, the temperature is wrong, and there is no ship to return to. The column endures.

High mountain passes. The sailors of Umbar are performing a forced march through terrain that their entire professional lives have trained them to avoid. They are managing. They are also visibly miserable.
Snow and altitude. The corsairs were built for water and warm southern shores, not frozen passes. The column continues because the contract requires it. The contract is doing a lot of work right now.
Desert terrain — the Bardings of Dale are as far from the Long Lake as they could be. No water, no fish, no familiar landmarks. The practical Barding mind notes the deficit and keeps walking.
The desert is not Long Lake country. Dale's soldiers manage it with the same practical grit they bring to all problems — but the grit is being spent faster than it would be on familiar ground.
Sand and sun and the complete absence of anything that smells like Esgaroth. The Bardings of Dale are performing a professional feat of endurance. The ledger is not pleased.
The field is ours. Gondor's soldiers stand over the fallen in the specific quiet of men who know the cost and accept it. The White City asked for this, and this is what was given.

Victory for the sons of Númenor. The men clean their blades and check on their wounded before they check on themselves. This is what Gondorian victory looks like — thorough, dignified, and already thinking about the next watch.
The battle is won. A Gondorian win is never celebrated loudly — it is acknowledged and filed. The column reforms. The march continues toward whatever the next obligation demands.
The White City answers to you now. The weight of Gondor's legacy settles on your shoulders with the gravity of stone — there are worse things to carry, and no one has carried it longer or better.

Ruling Gondor is not a position one holds lightly. Every decision will be measured against centuries of Stewards and a King who came back after thousands of years. The standard is exactly as high as it sounds.
The keys of the Citadel are yours. The soldiers serve because they believe in the institution — and right now, you are the institution. Carry that with the weight it deserves.

Gondor's oath-service sits differently than other factions' vassalage. The sons of Númenor swear to protect, not merely to obey — the distinction matters, and the soldiers feel it in every order from above.
You serve a greater Gondorian authority. The White City has always had a chain of command longer than any individual ambition — finding your place in it is not diminishment. It is tradition.
Vassal service in Gondor's name means bearing the White Tower's standards into battles where the credit flows upward. The soldiers understand this. They have always understood this.

Gondor's soldiers fight for the idea of Gondor whether or not any king commands them. An independent Gondorian company carries the White City in its bones — no political arrangement changes what these men are.

Without kingdom or oath, the sons of Númenor still march as the sons of Númenor. Freedom from allegiance costs something in Gondor's culture — the soldiers feel the absence of structure, even as they move freely.

An unsworn Gondorian force is a rare thing. The culture of the White City tends toward order and obligation. These soldiers carry both without the framework — which means they carry them by will alone.
Nobody knows you yet. The soldiers of Gondor respect rank and record, and right now both columns are empty. The White City watches new commanders quietly, completely, and with a very long memory.

Your name has not yet reached the rosters of Gondor's celebrated captains. That is not a permanent condition, merely a current one. The men serve regardless — but they are noting what you do with the opportunities ahead.
The gates of Minas Tirith open to many commanders. Your name has not yet attached itself to any particular gate or battle. That is the starting position. Everything from here is what you make of it.

Your name is beginning to travel. A Gondorian soldier returning from patrol mentioned it in the mess. That is how Gondor's legends begin — not with ceremony, but with the ordinary transmission of reputation.
Word of your deeds has reached at least one corner of the White City. The soldiers of Gondor are conservative with their respect — when they begin to speak your name, something has been earned.

The ledgers of Gondor's military historians have a new entry. It is short. It will grow. The sons of Númenor have been recording the deeds of captains since before memory — your entry is now among them.
The soldiers of the White City know your name and your battles. Gondorian martial reputation travels through the ranks thoroughly, accurately, and with footnotes. Yours has arrived.
Your deeds have earned a place in Gondor's ongoing account of the campaign age. Not a permanent place yet — but a place that will be cited when captains compare notes from the Pelennor to Ithilien.

Word of your name has reached officers who had not heard it before, and they are asking questions. In Gondor, the questions themselves are a form of recognition — they mean someone with authority is paying attention.

The songs are being written. Gondor's bards have a particular genre for commanders whose deeds exceed the standard measurement — they are writing yours in it now. The White City does not mythologise lightly.

Your deeds will outlast you in the records of the White City. Future captains will study what you did in this age. That is not a compliment Gondor gives freely — it is an accounting, and the accounting favours you.

The annals of Gondor are long and the standard for legendary inclusion is high. You have met it. The Tower of Guard will remember your name when everyone who knew you personally has been dust for centuries.
The White City's general is wounded. The soldiers maintain their formation and composure — this is Gondorian discipline from the inside. Nobody shows the fear. Everyone feels it.
A wound on a Gondorian commander travels through the ranks as information before it travels as emotion. The men note it, assess it, adjust, and say nothing directly. The silence says everything.

The sons of Númenor have served wounded commanders before. They serve the wounded as they serve the whole — with the Gondorian combination of loyalty, discretion, and the unspoken expectation that you will recover and continue.

The Rohirrim have won the field and the horses know it. The riders whoop once — a sharp Rohirric sound that means something different from infantry celebration — and then they're already scouting the next ridge.
Victory under the banner of the Riddermark. The Riders celebrate the way they do everything: briefly, loudly, and then immediately practical. There's a horse to see to and a column to reform.
The thunder of hooves receding, the field to the Rohirrim. Théoden's heirs mark the win by standing in their stirrups and looking to the horizon — already asking what comes next.

Ruling the Riddermark means being the horn that calls every Rider. The Rohirrim follow strength they can see and ride beside — the authority of the Mark's leader is earned every single day on horseback.
The Mark rides at your word. The Éored captains will follow your summons with the trust of people who read a leader by how they sit their horse. You sit yours well. They have noticed.

Lord of the Riddermark. That is not a title that comes with comfort — it comes with the expectation that you can outride, outfight, and outlast everyone who follows you. They are watching to see if you can.
The Mark bows to a greater authority but never fully bends. Rohirric vassalage is oath and alliance, not submission — the Riders serve their lord's cause as their own, with full Rohirric intensity.
Oath-bound service sits in the Rohirrim's culture as something between honour and obligation. The Riders fulfil the oath not because they must, but because breaking one is worse than dying.
The Riddermark lends its speed to a greater army. The soldiers ride as hard for an ally's war as for their own — the oath makes it their own, and the Rohirrim take their oaths at face value.

Without crown or allegiance, the Riders of the Mark ride as free men. There is something the Rohirrim understand deeply about freedom of movement — unsworn, they are more themselves than most cultures are with all the trappings of authority.
A Rohirric company without allegiance is not leaderless. It follows the leader it chose rather than the one it was assigned. The distinction matters enormously to the Riders of the Mark.

Free hooves on open plain — this is the Riddermark at its most itself. No oath, no king's summons, just the horizon and the question of which direction to ride toward it. The Rohirrim are content with this.

The Riddermark respects those who have proven themselves on horseback. You have not yet proven yourself by Rohirric standards. The Riders are watching with the patient assessment of men who commit fast when they do.
Unknown in the songs of the Riddermark. The Rohirrim remember heroes in verse and story — your story hasn't started. The horses don't know your name yet either. Both are paying attention.
In the mess halls of Edoras, no one tells your story yet. The Riders follow a capable commander they don't know — but they don't speak the name until the deeds justify speaking.

Your name has been mentioned in the Riddermark. Not sung yet — but mentioned. In the oral tradition of the Rohirrim, that is how songs begin. A captain whose name travels by mouth is on the way to something larger.

Word of your deeds has found its way to the Éored captains. The Rohirrim don't tell stories about people they don't respect — the fact that they're telling yours means something has been done worth the telling.
The Riders are beginning to know who you are. In Rohirric culture, being known means being worth the knowing. The men of the Mark decide that with the same directness they apply to everything.
The plains carry your name now. A Rohirric reputation travels on horseback — fast and far. The captains of the Mark speak your deeds as reference points now.
Songs about you are being composed in the great halls of Edoras. They are not finished yet. They will be. The Rohirrim compose songs for commanders they believe in, not merely respect.
The men of the Riddermark know your story. They tell it the way they tell all important things — riding, at speed, with enough detail to be accurate and enough drama to be worth repeating.

The great songs of the Riddermark have a new verse with your name in it. Your name will be spoken by Riders who never knew you, used as shorthand for a standard worth meeting. That is as permanent as anything gets.

Your legend has entered the canon of the Riddermark. The Riders will tell your story for generations — not because you asked, but because what you did was the kind of thing that the songs need to carry.

The bards of Edoras are still composing. The soldiers already know the ending — legendary. In Rohirric culture, this is as permanent as stone and considerably faster. The Mark remembers its heroes completely.

The Rider is wounded. The Rohirrim register it as they register everything — quickly, practically, and with immediate recalibration of the day's plans. The horses sense it before the soldiers say it. Both adjust.
A wounded Rohirric commander is not a defeated one. The Riders of the Mark ride hurt when they must — the culture allows no other position — but there is a specific watchfulness in the column today.

The Riddermark's leader carries a wound. The Éored captains are riding closer than usual, with the practical solidarity of cavalry who know that the next fight may require someone to cover for the commander's limitations.
The battle is done and the Bardings count their losses with the same ledger-mind they apply to profit. Dale won this one. The entry goes in the victory column. The next question is cost and margin.
A field taken by the soldiers of Esgaroth. The Bardings celebrate with the subdued satisfaction of pragmatic people — not loudly, but thoroughly. The numbers work out. The column moves on.
The Long Lake's people have won the field. King Brand's soldiers secure the area with the brisk efficiency of a trading city waking up. Victory is noted. Now back to work.

King of Dale — a position carrying the specific gravity of a rebuilt city. Every leader since Smaug has governed in the shadow of what rebuilding cost. You carry that weight now, and the people of Esgaroth are watching.
Ruling Dale means stewarding the Long Lake's most improbable success story. The city was ash in living memory — every decision is measured against whether it builds on that recovery or risks it.

The throne of Dale is yours. The merchants, the fishermen, the soldiers — all wondering whether you understand this city was rebuilt by determined practical work that doesn't respond well to grandiosity. Govern accordingly.

Dale's service to a greater king is transactional in the best sense — oath-bound allies, not reluctant subjects. They bring their skills and Long Lake provisions to the greater cause and expect the arrangement honoured.

Barding vassalage carries the quality of a trading partnership sealed with an oath. The soldiers of Dale will fulfil their obligations completely — and they will keep track of whether the greater power fulfils its obligations in return.
The Bardings serve with the same practical thoroughness they bring to commercial contracts. The oath is binding. The terms are understood. The performance will be measured and remembered.

An independent company from Esgaroth operates on a simple principle: if the arrangement isn't serving Dale's interests, the arrangement ends. The soldiers are not cynical — they are practical, and practical is its own integrity.
Without a king's authority above them, the Bardings navigate the world as they always have — by the route that makes the most sense, toward the outcome that costs the least and gains the most.
Dale's soldiers operate freely and know it. The independence is noticed, appreciated, and will be leveraged — the Bardings of Esgaroth have always known how to make their freedom work for them.
Your name doesn't appear in the Long Lake's network of rumour and report yet. The Bardings are patient recordkeepers — they will note your name when your deeds justify the entry.
The ledgers of Dale don't have your story yet. They will. The Bardings have been keeping track of the world since before Smaug, and they will keep track of you when there is enough to track.
The merchants of Esgaroth note everything that moves through their city. Yours has not yet arrived at their counting-houses. That is simply a matter of time and deeds.

Your name has reached the trading routes around the Long Lake. In Dale's information network — which is extensive, because trade requires information — being noticed means your reputation has real weight in at least one direction.

Word of your deeds has arrived in Esgaroth's marketplace, which is also the marketplace of reputation. The Bardings have begun to associate your name with results. That is the beginning of something significant.

The merchants of Dale are asking about you. In Barding culture, being the subject of commercial inquiry is a form of distinction — it means someone with resources has decided you're worth understanding.
Your name carries weight in the Long Lake region. The Bardings use it as a reference point in conversation — shorthand that requires no elaboration. That is Barding recognition at its most genuine.
The trade routes carry your story now. In Dale's culture, reputation travels the same roads as goods — and right now, your reputation is moving faster and further than most of what those roads carry.
Dale's soldiers speak your deeds in the casual way of people who find them useful for comparison. That is the Barding version of a legend in progress — practical, referenced, and steadily growing.
King Brand's city will remember your name — not just in official records, but in the stories the fishermen and merchants tell. That is the form of permanence the Long Lake's people trust most.

Your legend has entered Esgaroth's oral history. The Bardings will tell your story alongside the story of the city's rebuilding — you've become part of the larger narrative about survival and what it costs.
The tales of Dale now include yours. Future generations will learn your name alongside Girion's and Brand's — part of the city's story of how it endured and what it endured with.
The Barding commander is wounded. The soldiers note it and adjust — practically, without drama, because drama doesn't help anyone. The column continues. The ledger accounting continues.

A wound on King Brand's soldier is a problem to be solved, not mourned. The Bardings bring the same efficient management to a wounded commander that they bring to a disrupted supply line: assess, adapt, move forward.
Dale's leader is hurt. The Bardings apply their field knowledge efficiently and continue — a wounded commander is a problem, problems have solutions, the solution is in progress.

The Noldor have prevailed. The battlefield is cleared with Elvish thoroughness — every fallen accounted for, every prisoner assessed, every option for mercy considered before the march resumes. Victory means nothing is wasted.

Imladris has won the field. The Noldor stand amid the aftermath with the serene competence of people who have participated in the long defeat and the long victory alike, and who know neither is final.

The Elves of Rivendell have taken the day. They do not celebrate — they observe. Elrond's soldiers stand in the aftermath with the equanimity of creatures old enough to know victory and defeat are rarely absolute.

Ruling in the tradition of Imladris means governing with the patience of the ageless. Elrond held Rivendell through three ages — the standard of leadership he set is not a modest one, and the Noldor know it.

The hidden valley looks to you as it once looked to the Lord of Rivendell. The Elves are not subjects who require governance — they are a community that requires wisdom. They expect yours to justify their confidence.
Leading the Noldor means carrying the weight of the oldest living memory on earth. Your decisions will be measured against three ages of Elven experience. That is not encouraging — it is accurate.

The Noldor serve with the grace of people who choose their obligations with care. Elrond's soldiers are not natural vassals — they are natural leaders serving a cause they have judged worth serving. The difference is felt in everything.

Imladris in service to a greater authority — a rare alignment of Elvish inclination and external need. The Noldor fulfil the role with complete competence and the persistent awareness that they could be doing this more efficiently.
The soldiers of Rivendell serve their oath with the same meticulous attention they give to the lembas-making. An obligation entered is an obligation honoured — the Noldor do not do things partially.

Without allegiance, the Noldor of Rivendell operate as they always preferred — by their own counsel, toward their own ends, with the patient certainty of people who have outlasted every political arrangement ever offered to them.

The Elves of Imladris unaffiliated with any greater power are, in a practical sense, more purposeful than the Elves of Imladris with allegiances. They have nothing to explain to anyone. Elrond never truly needed alliances.

Free of kingdom and king, Rivendell's soldiers move as they were made to move — gracefully, purposefully, and without the friction of obligations that were never entirely natural to them in the first place.

The Noldor of Rivendell have a very long memory for the deeds of mortals — which means they note carefully when a mortal's deeds have not yet justified their attention. Your name has not reached Imladris in any meaningful way.
Elrond's halls have hosted the great and the obscure alike. The Elves note the difference — not unkindly, but clearly. Your name is not yet in the category of the great. The category is not closed.
The histories of Rivendell do not yet carry your name. The Noldor begin recording a mortal's deeds when the deeds become worth recording. The threshold is high. The opportunity is open.

Your name has reached the ears of the Noldor. They have good ears, and good memories for what they hear — being noticed by Rivendell means being noticed by creatures with three ages of heroism to compare against.
Imladris has begun to speak your name in council. The Elves of Rivendell do not discuss mortals who are not worth discussing, and the discussions are thorough.
The long memory of the Noldor has made an entry for you. Brief so far — but Rivendell's entries grow, because the Elves who keep them live long enough to see every story through to its end.

The Noldor have placed you among the mortals worth knowing. The criteria are exacting and the membership is distinguished. You are in it now, and the Elves are paying the attention they pay to things they have decided matter.

Your deeds are being discussed in Imladris. The Noldor compare them to the deeds of ages past — not to diminish them, but because that is the only frame of reference the Elves of Rivendell have. Your deeds are holding up.

The soldiers of Rivendell speak your name with the specific Elvish respect that means they have assessed your worth and found it genuine. For creatures who have known Beren and Tuor, that assessment is informed.

The lore-masters of Imladris are writing about you. That means your deeds will persist in the most reliable archive in Middle-earth — the long memory of the Noldor, who forget nothing they decide is worth remembering.

Rivendell's records will carry your name past the end of the age. The Elves have kept the world's account since the First Age — your legend is now part of that account, which is as close to permanent as anything gets.
The Noldor have placed you among the mortals whose stories belong to the greater history of the world. That is not flattery — it is classification. And the Elves of Rivendell classify with precision.

The Noldor's commander is wounded. The Elves respond with the practical care and the deep sadness of creatures for whom mortal injury is a reminder of things they find it difficult not to think about constantly.

Imladris's leader carries a wound. The Elves attend to it with everything their ancient healing skill allows — and then they continue the march, because the only response to mortal fragility is to be careful and keep moving.

A wound on the leader of Rivendell's company is a medical problem and a philosophical one. The Noldor solve the first with lore and skill. The second they carry quietly, alongside everything else they carry quietly.

The wood-elves have taken the field. They celebrate by melting back into the nearest cover, checking the forest, and acknowledging the victory in the way of creatures who were never entirely comfortable in the open.

Victory for the Silvan Elves. The Mirkwood warriors secure their kills and vanish into tree-shadow with an efficiency that makes the whole battle look like it happened somewhere slightly apart from reality.

Thranduil's soldiers have won. They are already in the trees. Whether this is a tactical withdrawal, a celebration, or simply how they prefer to exist after combat may not be a distinction that matters.

Leading Mirkwood means leading a people intensely attached to their forest. The Silvan Elves follow a ruler who understands the wood — not as a political entity but as a living, present thing shaping every decision in its shadow.

The throne of Mirkwood is a precarious honour. The great forest is darker than it was, the shadow has never fully left, and the Silvan Elves need a leader who can hold the line between those who retreat and those who endure.

You lead the wood-elves now. Thranduil held this position for an age and made it look effortless, which means the Silvan Elves have very specific expectations about effortlessness. They are watching to see whether you meet them.

The wood-elves in service to a greater power is an uncomfortable arrangement for creatures of independent forest instinct. They fulfil the obligation — completely and with considerable personal reservations they don't express.

Mirkwood's alliance with a greater authority means the Silvan Elves are operating at a distance from the forest that doesn't entirely suit them. They manage it with the resilience of a people who have been managing a dark forest for centuries.
The forest-folk serve with their particular version of loyalty — thorough in practice, independent in spirit, and never entirely without the sense that they would rather be somewhere with more trees.

The wood-elves unaffiliated with any kingdom are the wood-elves as they were made to be. Free of obligation, they move through the world with the easy mastery of creatures who never needed anyone else's authority to justify their presence.

Mirkwood's soldiers without allegiance are in their natural state — moving through cover, trusting no open ground, answering to no summons except the forest's own. This is what Thranduil always wanted for his people.
Unsworn and unaligned, the Silvan Elves are at their most themselves. The forest-folk have always been more comfortable with roots than with chains of command, and right now there are only roots.

The Silvan Elves of Mirkwood are watching. They watch everything — it is how they survived when the great spiders moved in and the darkness came. Your deeds have not yet given them reason to speak your name.

Your name has not yet reached the great halls beneath the Lonely Mountain — Thranduil's people hear news slowly by choice, filtering what matters from what doesn't. You haven't risen to the level of matters yet.

The wood-elves don't know who you are yet. They barely knew who anyone was until those people gave them reason to. The forest demands attention, and outsiders get what's left after the forest is seen to.

Your name has filtered through the Mirkwood information network — which is extensive, patient, and operates through creatures that are almost impossible to follow through the trees. You've been noticed. The Silvan Elves have decided you're worth the attention.

The wood-elves are talking about you. That is itself notable — they don't waste conversation on people they haven't assessed. Your deeds have cleared the assessment threshold, which is more than most people manage.

Mirkwood knows your name now. The specific way the Silvan Elves carry information means your reputation arrived as a whisper through the forest — quiet, accurate, and now in every Elven ear in the wood.
The songs of Mirkwood carry your name. The wood-elves have their own tradition of remembering — lighter than Rivendell's careful histories, wilder, better suited to the forest. You're in it now.

Thranduil's people speak your deeds in the way they speak things they consider worth remembering — with the particular quality of creatures who remember everything and only repeat the things that deserve repeating.

Your reputation has reached the treetops. In Mirkwood's culture, being discussed in the high flets means your name has achieved something — a recognition the Silvan Elves give only when genuinely moved.
The Silvan Elves of Mirkwood will carry your name in their songs when the great forest is long changed. The wood-elves remember what they love, and they do not love lightly.

Your legend has entered the oral tradition of the Silvan Elves. It will change shape as it travels — that is the nature of forest memory, which grows around things rather than preserving them in amber.

The wood-elves of Mirkwood have made you part of their world. The Silvan Elves don't have much use for the outside world, and choosing to remember someone from it means something enormous by their standards.
The commander of Mirkwood's company is wounded. The Silvan Elves respond with the silent, intense concern of forest-folk who have learned to take nothing for granted about the continuation of life.

A wound on the wood-elf leader. The Silvan Elves move closer without making a show of it — the protective instinct of a people who have lost a great deal to darkness and have decided not to lose more if they can help it.
The forest-folk watch their wounded commander with the vigilance of creatures who know, from long experience, that wounds heal — but that the time between wound and healing is when things go wrong.

The Galadhrim have won the field. The victory settles over them like the Golden Wood's own quiet — not triumphant, not relieved, but present. They have done what was asked with the grace that is always asked of them.
Lothlórien's soldiers have prevailed. They stand in the aftermath with Galadhrim composure — the victory is registered, the cost is known, the march continues.

The Lady's soldiers have taken the day. They begin immediately to account for their fallen, their wounded, and their prisoners — in that order, which is the Galadhrim order, and which says something about their priorities.

Leading the Galadhrim means living up to Galadriel. The Lady set the standard for Lothlórien's rulership over three ages. The Elves of the Golden Wood are watching whether humility leads or paralysis does.

The rulership of Lothlórien carries the weight of the most beautiful thing still standing. Every decision made on behalf of the Golden Wood is measured against the question of whether it preserves or diminishes that beauty.

You lead the Golden Wood now. The mallorn trees have stood here since before the Second Age and the Galadhrim have protected them that long. Lead as though you intend to be still doing this when the next age begins.

Lothlórien's service to a greater authority means the Golden Wood's wisdom and strength are offered in support of a cause the Lady would judge worthy. The Galadhrim serve with the quality of people who have chosen their obligation — chosen it with everything they are.

The soldiers of the Golden Wood fight with their full Galadhrim capability and a constant gentle awareness that they are carrying something irreplaceable into the world's dangers. They accept the risk. They never stop being aware of it.

Vassal service for the Lady's people is not diminishment — it is extension. The Golden Wood reaches further when its soldiers march in a greater cause. The Galadhrim carry Lothlórien's light into territory it would not otherwise touch.

The Galadhrim unbound by allegiance move with the unhurried certainty of people who answer to a standard no king can equal or replace. The Lady's soldiers don't need a kingdom to justify their presence — they are Lothlórien.

Without kingdom or oath, the soldiers of the Golden Wood carry their identity more purely than almost any other army. The Galadhrim were never fully of the world's political arrangements — freedom from them is simply returning to their natural condition.

Free of the world's claims, the Golden Wood's soldiers are their most themselves. The Galadhrim have always needed the forest more than the forest needed a king. Right now they have the forest in their hearts and nothing above them.

The Lady of Lothlórien has seen the future and the past with equal clarity. Your future is not yet clear enough to have been observed. The Galadhrim watch new commanders with the patient attention of creatures who can wait as long as the truth requires.
Your name has not yet reached the ear of the Golden Wood in any significant way. The Galadhrim pay attention to everything that matters, and eventually everything that matters becomes clear.
The flets of Lothlórien do not yet carry your name. The wood-walkers of the Golden Wood note what passes through their domain — you will be noted when there is something worth the noting.
The Galadhrim have begun to speak your name. The Elves of Lothlórien do not speak names that don't deserve speaking, and the decision to speak yours means something has been observed and evaluated.
Your deeds have reached the Golden Wood. The Lady's people hear news the way the forest hears wind — completely and from every direction. Your name has arrived among them and has been assessed.
Lothlórien notes your name now. The Galadhrim are careful with what they carry in their long memory — being among the things they carry means you have done something worth the carrying.

The songs of Lothlórien have made space for your deeds. The Galadhrim are the most discerning audience in Middle-earth — their songs have been composed since the First Age, and the standard for inclusion is three ages of comparison material.

Your name is spoken in the mallorn-light of the Golden Wood. The Galadhrim use it as shorthand for a specific quality — the shorthand itself is a form of honour, a compression of everything you've done into something the Elves carry readily.

The Lady's people speak of you with the specific Galadhrim approval that is difficult to earn and impossible to fake. You have earned it. The Golden Wood remembers the things it approves of until the trees themselves forget.

The lore of Lothlórien carries your name past the age's end. The Galadhrim have been composing the world's most careful account of the ages since Amon Lanc stood empty — your legend is now part of that account.

Your deeds are part of the Golden Wood's memory now. The mallorn trees may yet stand when everything else built by mortal hands has returned to earth — and in their shadow, the Elves will still tell your story.

The legend the Galadhrim have made of you will travel with the Elves to wherever the Elves go. That is a form of immortality given by the accumulated weight of your own deeds, which the Lady only observed.

The Galadhrim's commander carries a wound. The Lady's soldiers attend to it with the full weight of their healing knowledge and a profound, specific sadness — the Elves of Lothlórien have the deepest understanding of what it costs when something beautiful is harmed.

A wound on the leader of the Golden Wood's company. The Galadhrim heal with everything they have, because to Elves of Lothlórien's tradition, wounds on those they protect are not merely tactical problems. They are personal.

The soldiers of the Golden Wood are quietly, completely focused on their wounded commander. The Galadhrim manage their concern by transforming it into action — the most thorough healing, the most careful watch, the most attentive presence.

King Under the Mountain — the title that Thorin reclaimed and what came after. The crown of Erebor carries the weight of a people who were exiled for decades and returned to rebuild something extraordinary. Leading them means understanding what that cost.
